speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ROYAL ASSENT TO PROVINCIAL BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table two copies of order in council P.C. 1961-675, dated May 5, in which His Excellency the Governor General by and with the advice of Her Majesty the Queen's privy council for Canada declares his assent to Bill No. 56 of the legislature of Saskatchewan passed during the present year and which was reserved by the lieutenant governor of Saskatchewan for the signification of the pleasure of the Governor General in accordance with the terms of the British North America Act.
In view of the importance of the constitutional issue involved, and with the leave of the house, I should like to place on the record the text of this order in council. It is a relatively short one. Leaving out the preliminaries and commencing with the preamble it reads as follows:
Whereas Bill No. 56 entitled "The Mineral Contracts Alteration Act, 1961" passed by the legislature of the province of Saskatchewan at the first session of the fourteenth legislature of the province of Saskatchewan, was reserved on the 8th day of April, 1961, by his honour the lieutenant governor of Saskatchewan for the signification of the pleasure of the Governor General;
And whereas the lieutenant governor, in transmitting the bill, gave as his reasons for reserving it
(a)	that the bill, in his view, was ultra vires the legislature, and
(b)	that the bill was not in the national interest;
And whereas it is the established policy in these
matters to consider first the question of whether the bill is within the competence of the legislature to enact and second the question of whether it is in conflict with national policy or interest, and if these two questions be resolved favourably, to recommend that assent be given unless the bill is otherwise objectionable;
And whereas the Minister of Justice has examined the bill and has considered the reasons given by his honour the lieutenant governor for the reservation thereof, and he is of the opinion, with respect to the first question, that the bill is within the competence of the legislature to enact; that, with respect to the second question, the minister has considered the authorities and precedents, and is of the opinion that the expression "conflict with national policy or interest" does not relate solely to a difference of principle or point of view, but must include matters of practical or physical effect, and that in this sense the bill is not in conflict with national policy or interest;
And whereas the question of whether the bill is otherwise objectionable, being a matter that
involves considerations other than legal, has been considered by His Excellency's advisers as a whole, and the conclusion has been reached that the nature of the bill is not such as to warrant departure from the normal course of recommending assent;
Wherefore His Excellency the Governor General, by and with the advice of the Queen's privy council for Canada, is pleased hereby to declare his assent to the said bill.
The house will recall that Hon. Frank Bastedo, lieutenant governor of Saskatchewan, reserved this bill, and did so without instructions from or consultation with the federal government. I have no hesitation in saying that had there been such consultation my colleagues and I would have recommended to the Governor General that the lieutenant governor be instructed not to reserve the bill.
I should call your attention, sir, and that of the house to the fact that in 1882 the governor general in council, in a minute of council transmitted to the lieutenant governors of each province, noted:
The lieutenant governor is not warranted in reserving any measure for the assent of the governor general on the advice of his ministers. He should do so in his capacity of a dominion officer only, and on instructions from the Governor General. It is only in a case of extreme necessity that a lieutenant governor should without such instructions exercise his discretion as a dominion officer in reserving a bill. In fact, with facility of communication between the dominion and provincial governments such a necessity can seldom if ever arise.
That was in 1882. In view of the development of communications since, it is evident that nowadays there should be ample opportunity for lieutenant governors to confer with the federal government before reserving a bill. I should point out that while no formal instructions have yet been given to lieutenant governors to reserve a bill unless upon specific instructions, my colleagues and I are now considering whether such formal instructions should be given.
In so far as the substance and other aspects of the bill in question are concerned, they are properly, of course, the concern of the governor general in council; and I feel that instead of going into detail, if there is any discussion to take place on this matter it might well be postponed until the estimates of the privy council are before the house unless naturally, in the meantime, opportunity arises for discussion.

subtopic: RUANDA-URUNDI  APPOINTMENT OF CANADIAN MEMBER OF SPECIAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to announce the appointment of the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin) to the special United Nations commission of judicial review for the Belgian trust territory of Ruanda-Urundi.
The territory is a small, densely populated area lying landlocked in equatorial Africa between the republic of the Congo-Leopoldville-to the west, Uganda to the north and Tanganyika to the east and south. A former German colony, since 1919 it has been administered by Belgium, first as a mandate of the league of nations and subsequently as a trust territory of the United Nations.
On April 21 the general assembly adopted by a large majority, which included Canada, a resolution giving Belgium specific directives in respect of the administration of the territory and its evolution to independence. The resolution also contained a provision for the implementation of a general amnesty and the establishment of a special three nation commission to review a number of cases of persons convicted of grave crimes with a view to securing their release from prison or return from exile. Canada, together with Brazil and Tunisia, was elected to serve on this commission, which is expected to leave this month on a journey of approximately three weeks to Belgium and Ruanda-Urundi and to submit a report to the United Nations prior to legislative elections in the territory scheduled for August of this year. The costs of the commission will, of course, be borne by the United Nations.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Charlevoix is well qualified to take this assignment. He has broad legal and political experience, and has concerned himself particularly with international affairs. In 1958 he was a member of the Canadian delegation to the NATO parliamentary association meeting in London, and during the fifteenth session of the United Nations general assembly which has just been completed he served as Canadian representative both in the legal committee and also in the trusteeship committee, which has been considering the Ruanda-Urundi item. This hon. member has made a splendid contribution to the work of the United Nations during its last session.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: 279. Departmental administration including Canada's share of the expenses of the "resources for tomorrow" conference, $1,105,390.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before closing last night the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River raised a point as to whether the members of the committee were not getting rather short shrift from the minister, in that his replies to questions raised earlier in the discussion were to be given in letter form rather than rebutted or answered in this forum. I think the member for Kenora-Rainy River, and other members,
[Mr. Pickersgill.J
might have support for their argument in that the minister, seemed to take such an inordinate time to reply to the hon. member for Port Arthur. I make no claim that the points I raised had any particular priority or importance over those raised by any other hon. member.
I think the minister's reaction, despite the fact that he credited me with not being personal, was for that very reason. He thought my criticism was personal. Perhaps I should have made it clear that in my comments on the minister I was really questioning or blaming the Prime Minister in the selection of a minister. It seems to be a ritual here, and I suppose a very nice ritual, that when a man takes over a portfolio everybody is appropriately sweet and nice.
I should like to assure the minister that to me he ranks with Abou Ben Adhem in the sense that I am sure he leads all the rest in those fine qualities of charity, industry, humanity and all the rest. But despite all this I honestly feel that in the serried ranks behind the Prime Minister there might possibly have been found-I do not want to be invidious and select a few names-a man who could have given this particular department more dynamic drive. If this is unfair or unkind, well, so be it.
I should like to assure the minister that my remarks were no reflection upon his industry or his capacity in the past. I am sorry that, from the length of the reply he made, there would seem to be an indication that my remarks touched on a sensitive nerve, and that he took the opportunity while talking about petulant pedagogues-although he did take a bit of a cut at himself-to attack the teaching profession. I should like to point out to the minister that I do not think of myself as a teacher at the present time. I happen to be a politician and will be until this particular parliament dissolves. Then if I want to go back to teaching-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You are still in an ivory tower.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
No; my criticisms were made not as a teacher but as a politician, and they stand in that position. In a sense he rebutted a few of the points I made. For example, in so far as the resources for tomorrow conference is concerned, the minister started with an inaccuracy. I was not the only hon. member who referred to the resources for tomorrow conference. I would give him the hon. member for Kootenay West, who talked quite a bit about his views on the matter. The minister then said that I should go forth and carry the word about the resources

for tomorrow conference. I suggest to him that there were a great many members speaking in this debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I used the plural, and I included all members in that challenge.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I point out that at least two members of this group have done their best to publicize this conference. I further point out that I gave several speeches in my own constituency to groups of professional forresters last year, and I can assure the minister that those foresters had not heard about the conference previously and those meetings were well reported by newspaper, radio and television. I believe the area I represent, in the main, knows probably more about this conference, which I consider very important, than other areas.
I come back to the point I made that if in April, 1961, the editor of a prominent business magazine had never heard of the resources for tomorrow conference, there is a fault somewhere in the publicizing of it. One of the points made was that this was an integrated undertaking and was not the sole responsibility of the minister. I quite agree, but I should like to point out to him that we have the minister of lands and forests in Ontario who, I understand, is on the committee. I have many criticisms of Mr. Spooner, but I recognize that he is an able, I might even say crafty, person. In so far as the minister for Manitoba is concerned, who I believe is Mr. Gurney Evans, I would say he is as qualified a cabinet minister as we have in all the provinces. I have already made my bow to the contributions made by Mr. Levesque who, I think, is doing a grand job in this particular context.
It is for this very reason, when I look at three men with this much ability, that I want to see the federal government take a stronger role. I want to see a strong man in there to make sure we get something from the conference. This is the challenge I put to the minister. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, there is a common view in this house that if there is a weak minister in one department the opposition should be joyful. I have never looked at it that way. Despite the fact that we may be here as opposition members, I want to see whatever government is in power give good administration, with lots of dynamic force and lots of drive. This has been the basis of my objection, and I reiterate my disappointment.
In so far as the part of this department which I thought was of most importance is concerned, it has been removed now and has its own substance in the Department of Forestry. I should like to come back to what I felt was the key point of my criticisms,
Supply-Northern Affairs and I believe the minister suggested that I said there was nothing going on in the north. I indicated nothing of the kind. My point was that there was not enough going on in the south. I point out to the minister that he is the minister not only of northern affairs but of national resources. I point out to him that he can be pictured with all the Eskimo and Indian children in the world in his loving embrace, or watching what they are doing, but his department has other responsibilities as well.
I suggest to him that he read a brief- if he has not a copy of it I will send it to him-written by C. M. Campbell of Vancouver, British Columbia entitled "Canada: A Nation of Economic Liars". Mr. Campbell is a mining engineer who has been spending many years trying to convince Canadians that they talk too much about their unlimited resources and do not look closely enough at the realities of the situation. I pointed out one reality to the minister in my own area. He has, in his department, a map showing a road projected from somewhere north of lake Nipigon and running up toward Churchill in a certain direction. I know that road is not projected at the present time but is only presented as a preliminary idea in relation to a survey of that area.
In my own area, which contains 40,000 square miles, we want roads. We want the federal government to take the lead in the roads to resources program. However, in addition we still have this southern perimeter that has not been developed with the appropriate roads. The minister suggested that I said there was nothing going on in the north and this was a criticism, but my point was that the minister has a responsibility to keep his eyes on the south, too.
I should like to point out something that may give point to this criticism. There is a story in Time magazine for April 14, 1961, which I should like to put on the record, Mr. Chairman. It reads:
Canada's energetic trade and commerce minister George Hees is not the man to bury himself in his own office, unaware of what goes on around him. His latest interest is the national parks. Travelling to lake Louise to inaugurate a new ski lift, Hees schussed down a slope, slued to a stop, and announced that he intended to speak to northern affairs and national resources minister Walter Dinsdale about opening up the parks for skiers.
"I have skied in a number of places in Europe and Canada, but this is the finest skiing I have had anywhere," said Hees amiably. "It's ridiculous for Canadians to be going to Aspen, Sun Valley and Squaw Valley when they have skiing like this at their back door."
Dinsdale just as amiably agreed that his cabinet man might have something. Added Dinsdale "I have got to get around and see the parks. I haven't seen any of them yet."

Supply-Northern Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in reference to that quotation may I say that I was never interviewed by any members of the press. That quotation is purely fictitious.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am glad to get that denial. Is the minister suggesting that he has been around to all the national parks?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have visited most of the national parks. This applies patricularly to the west. I shall visit the maritime parks as soon as the house rises.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am very much interested to have this comment. However, I will go on with the story:
Staff members of the national parks branch were less agreeable. Said one: "Private interests naturally are always putting pressure on the national parks system. Hees was going along. He is quite uninformed. Draw a 200 mile circle around Banff, and see what population it takes in. Your prospects aren't really outstanding." The six western ski developments operated by the parks branch are all at less than capacity.
What I should like to point out to the minister is this. The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria and another member from Nova Scotia pointed out the possibility of developing skiing in the maritimes. We have evidence that the national parks branch is interested in this field. I thought if the minister was giving a real review of his department, he would go into this question. I think it is an important one. Here we find that one of his own cabinet ministers is misinformed, according to this story. I do not want to put too much credence in this particular bible; I refer to Time magazine. I think this is an indication that the minister has been less than candid. He certainly has not given us a discursive or full account of his responsibility. He seemed to want to fasten upon the hon. member for Port Arthur instead of giving us some indication of what is going on in his department.
I should like to turn to another matter with regard to which I think he was wrong. In his comments directed to me he implied that I had suggested that the mines, forests and waters committee was ignored by the department. What I asked for was some indication that their recommendations had been followed. I should like to have action. It was not only last year but the year previous and the one previous to that, that this committee made recommendations.
I have gone through the annual report. The minister has his deputy minister right there with him, and he can tell him. I cannot find in the annual report any indication that the committee really had any effect at all upon the department. I know it did with regard to the forestry branch, but what about the museum and some of the recommendations
\ Mr. Fisher.]

there? What about other aspects of this fairly large department? I should like to know what the result has been. I think this assembly deserves this information in an itemized account. What was the detailed reaction to the recommendations of the committee?
I think the minister misinterpreted completely the approach I was taking. I thought this was a good committee, although when it was considering this department I thought it perhaps proceeded a bit too much to the north. However, I credit this procedure to the zeal of the hon. member for Yukon. In connection with this particular matter I might point out that the hon. member for Yukon has made the point a number of times that representation of the north in a parliamentary sense is inadequate. I point out to him and remind the minister-because I am sure he is interested in this point-that there are a number of constituencies in Canada proper which in population and area are comparable -when you realize that population is considered to be the most important factor in determining a constituency-to anything we have in Yukon or Mackenzie River. I know the area sizes. I should like to give the hon. member an example.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would mind my pointing out that I made no suggestion that representation in the north was inadequate. I pointed out that there was absolutely no representation in the Keewatin and Franklin districts of the north. That was my point.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to point out to the hon. member that parts of the constituency of Saguenay, the constituency of Churchill, the constituency of Port Arthur, and there is also one in Saskatchewan, in effect have no representation because of the population and where it is located. I have an area from Fort Severn in the northwest corner through to the tip of James bay and almost all the way to the C.N.R. railway line which it is almost impossible for me to cover as a member of parliament. I raise this matter here in order to indicate that the problem of the Arctic in terms of representation also has a parallel in the south.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: But the people in those areas have a vote. The people to whom I refer have no vote.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There were these same difficulties in Fort Severn. This was not the case in the last election. My emphasis here again is this. The minister is the minister of national resources. As minister of national resources he has a real challenge in the resources for tomorrow conference, namely to give an indication and a lead to the various provincial

legislatures; to lead, to persuade, to push, to get them moving in some kind of integrated plan of developing our resouces.
In relation to the resources for tomorrow conference, I should like to add that here there a tremendous emphasis on expertise. I should like to hear from the minister how it is planned to popularize the conference. A number of television programs have been set up. Arrangements have been made with the C.B.C. and the private stations to bring to the people what is being said there. Is an attempt going to be made to focus upon the provincial politicians who will be there in order to get from them some expression of opinion on how we are getting along on renewable resources? These are some of the things on which I should have appreciated comment much more than I appreciated having put on the record of the house some comments from an article that I had not read and for which I was not responsible.
Another point I should like to make to the minister in relation to this department is this. A number of years ago we had from the Massey commission recommendations that affected his department. Later on we had some consideration given to this problem by the mines, forest and waters committee. The minister has within his department what I might call some cultural branches. We know that the museum staff situation still has not been cleared up completely. At least we have not the balance in terms of language which hon. members from French Canada are talking about. When are we going to get changes in that branch to give us that balance? The minister did not talk about that matter at all. These are questions that I should like to hear answered in a situation such as this.
I do not want to take an inordinate amount of time. I suggest to the minister that in the future on his estimates he might consider being a bit more discursive and going into more detail. I think we would all appreciate that procedure much more than having a letter. I received a letter last year after these particular estimates were through. It stated that cost benefits analyses were going to be a definite part of the resources for tomorrow conference. This delighted me, because I think you cannot really look at resources without doing that kind of thing. But from following the conference and the way in which the matter was developing I know that the cost benefit analysis part of it almost slipped out of the proceedings altogether. I should have appreciated it much more if that very important statement by the former minister had been made in this house rather than in a letter to me.
In conclusion I should like to wish the minister all the best in his new portfolio. I do
Supply-Northern Affairs not think this parliament is going to last long enough for me to have the opportunity, but if I can in all honesty eat my own words, in so far as they have been critical, I give the hon. gentleman the assurance as fairly as I can that I shall be here to do it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Before this love feast between the hon. member for Port Arthur and the minister continues, I think I should protest on behalf of parliament against the offer which the minister made last night to the hon. member for Port Arthur, an offer which I think is absolutely outrageous. At the bottom of page 4391 of Hansard and on the following page I read these words:
If, as the hon. member for Port Arthur has indicated he does not feel he is making a worth while contribution in the house, I should like to suggest that there is tremendous scope in our educational program in the north and we would be glad to welcome him into our program when he retires from this honourable house.
Mr. Chairman, these posts in the north are supposed to be awarded by the civil service commission after competition on the basis of merit, and I think it is simply outrageous for a minister of the crown to seek to silence a timid member like the hon. member for Port Arthur by an offer which is an offer to break the law and which, in addition, probably comes close to an attempt at bribery.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I presume the hon. member is talking from experience when he says that applicants for these posts have to come before the civil service commission before they can be appointed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I hope so. I once appeared before a board myself, and I hope its decision was made on merit.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder if I could ask the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate whether he would advocate that the hon. member for Port Arthur should serve his apprenticeship to the hon. member for Essex East. That is one way to get into the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: How about asking the hon. member for Essex East whether he wants the hon. gentleman as an apprentice?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I indicated earlier to the minister that there were a number of questions that I wished to raise, and I think I shall raise them one by one and give the minister an opportunity to reply to them so that we shall not get mixed up. The first question-and it will not surprise the minister-is one which I approached originally by means of a question on the order paper

Supply

Northern Affairs last Thursday, when I asked the hon. gentleman, as reported at page 4047 of Hansard:
I should like to ask the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources whether his department has recently transferred its advertising account to a new advertising agency.
An hon. member suggested that the question be placed on the order paper. I thought that was a good suggestion, and subsequently I did place it on the order paper. In the meantime, however, the minister did me the courtesy to give me the following reply:
So far as I am aware, several agencies are handling the advertising account of the department. Those agencies have not been changed recently.
I then asked the minister whether he was aware that a story to this effect had appeared that day in the Winnipeg Free Press. Well, the story which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press that same day read as follows under the heading "Government Job for New Ad Firm":
The new federal minister of northern affairs has farmed out his department's entire national classified advertising account to an agency in his home town which went on a full-time basis, as an advertising agency, only last Friday.
The agency is the J. B. Neill advertising agency, operated by J. Barry Neill, formerly the owner of Barry Neill's clothing store.
Mr. Neill was active in the Young Progressive Conservative organization in Brandon.
All the classified advertising for the department headed by Hon. Walter Dinsdale, including national advertisements for northern teachers and other workers-
Too bad the hon. member for Port Arthur is not here to hear this.
is now being handled by a one man staff from a shared office in Brandon.
In Ottawa, the northern affairs department said Wednesday that the total classified advertising budget of their department in 1960 was $15,000.
Up until last Friday, the proprietor of the agency owned and operated a clothing store. He had a part-time advertising agency, covering some local accounts.
Friday the store was sold, and the agency became a full-time job for the proprietor. It operates from a shared office in a Brandon building, and the department of northern affairs account is the only national account in its files.
The proprietor of the agency said he and his secretary had no trouble handling the northern affairs account, even though it meant placing advertisements in papers across Canada, and some foreign advertising work.
The department of northern affairs pays a standard 15 per cent commission to the agency which handles its advertising.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Was this the civil service commission?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I also have here an article from the Brandon Daily Sun of the following day. This is headed "City Man gets Government Contract" and it reads:
The head of a one man advertising agency here has confirmed reports that he has received an account from the northern affairs department.


J. B. Neill, a former member of the Brandon city council, said he had been handling the advertising account since early January.
Mr. Neill, former owner of Barry Neill's men's wear store-
I do not think I need to read all this. It is information of the same kind that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, and I shall not repeat it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Not a good paper.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The Brandon Sun has never been a paper notorious for the support of any political party except the party of hon. gentlemen opposite.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, that is wrong. It is very fair and impartial.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not say it is not, though it is hard for me to understand how a paper which is fair and impartial could support hon. members on that side of the house. But I made no reflection on the paper, unless it is a reflection to say that a paper supports hon. gentlemen opposite. I have been acquainted in a general way with the Brandon Sun for about 45 years, and during all that time it has supported the Conservative party as far as I know. According to this story, Mr. Neill said he had made no representations to obtain the account. It just mysteriously reached him, apparently. Perhaps I may continue the quotation:
He said northern affairs minister Dinsdale, who represents Brandon-Souris riding in the commons, had approached him informally about taking the account last December.
The account was awarded the following month. Mr. Neill said he was notified that he was getting it in a letter from the purchasing division of the northern affairs department. Mr. Neill estimated total billings expected annually from the account will amount to anywhere from $10,000 to $25,000. His commission is 15 per cent of this.
He said the account was handled last year by Cooper Advertising of Saskatoon, but "account switches are very routine in the advertising business".
Well, it does seem to me that a government which has cast about it a mantle of righteousness should hardly be found in a situation of this kind. We remember very well the propaganda which the present Secretary of State for External Affairs used to circulate around the country, when he held his previous portfolio, to the effect that the Tories had abolished patronage, and the exhibition he made at that time.
While it may be that the handing out of an account which will only amount to $10,000 or $15,000 is not a very big thing-I would not assert for one minute that it was-it still has important implications. It is considered a big thing when $10,000 a year is paid to members of parliament for a whole year's work, but apparently it is a very small

thing when it is incidental to some advertising man who has gone into business full-time
only since last Friday.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is wrong.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Whether it is wrong or right, two very reputable newspapers report that he has sold his store and that he went into business full time last Friday; that would have been a week ago Friday.
What I found strange was the answer given by the minister to my first question. The minister said that in so far as he was aware, several agencies were handling the advertising accounts of the department, and that these agencies had not been changed recently. I am not suggesting that statement was not correct, because I suppose one can interpret the word "recently" in as sophistical a way as one likes, but I should have thought most ministers with experience would have assumed, since they had only been in the portfolio for a very short time, that any change of this kind, particularly in their home town, would be the kind of thing about which there would be a certain amount of interest.
It does seem to me, to put it in the most polite way I can, that in the answer of the minister given the other day in the house I will not say that he misled the house, but I would say his answer was disingenuous. It was not the kind of simple, straightforward answer we expect from a minister who prides himself on being simple and straightforward.
I do not know if this is part of the government's new campaign to aid small business. I do not know about the Cooper advertising agency, if that is the agency that had this business before, but perhaps it had become too big; perhaps it was not right politically, or perhaps because it was in Saskatchewan the minister thought, being from Manitoba instead of Saskatchewan, there should be a switch.
It does seem to me that this is a rather extraordinary performance. After all, if all that is required to place these advertisements is a stenographer with spare time, or someone in the clothing business, I wonder why someone in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources could not send them directly to the newspapers and thereby save the taxpayers the commission. It does not seem to me it is necessary to follow this procedure if it is as simple as suggested. If the advertising agency is designing the advertisements, wording them and earning something through its efforts, that is another question; but I cannot imagine that the agency would illustrate the advertisements with pictures of the schools in the north where teachers are required, and that 90205-6-279
Supply-Northern Affairs sort of thing. It seems to me this is purely a routine matter and I suggest that the committee is entitled to some explanation from the minister regarding this transaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have
listened very carefully to the words of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He is a man with long experience in this house, as well as in the civil service, and I am sure the expose he has just made, with all the infinite details and ramifications, indicates that when he was a responsible minister of the crown and also an official of the government, he was a master of intrigue. He has presented in his expose many new angles which, in my innocence, I had never even considered. I am interested to discover the source of the hon. member's information in respect of the particular problems he has raised.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The source of my information is the press of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I understand this information comes from that reputable paper, the Winnipeg Free Press.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And the Brandon Sun.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, with the support of that other reputable paper, the Brandon Sun, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has indicated.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has queried the accuracy of the reply I made to a question he asked in the house the other morning. I hope he has noticed that I said at that time that so far as I was aware there had been no change made recently in the advertising contracts of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I also went on to say that these contracts were of various types, the largest involved being those in respect of the tourist bureau, and that comes under my responsibility. The hon. member's question was worded in such a way as to give no particular indication of the advertising to which he referred.
I am happy to be able to assure him that when I gave my reply the information contained therein represented my knowledge of this subject at that time. There was no sinister intrigue involved, as he has implied.
In reference to the larger contracts, which amount to some $1,500,000, perhaps I should give this interesting piece of information. For some 15 years this total contract was held by one company, the Cockfield Brown Company. That company, I am sure, is not unknown to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate because of its close association with the party he represents in this house. I should like to inform the hon. member that
4414	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs the department of government looking after this large tourist bureau contract in 1957 divided that advertising business on an equitable basis among a series of companies so that everyone could be treated fairly in Canada. I am surprised that the hon. member has made such a mountain out of this molehill.
Last evening reference was made to a matter raised by the hon. member for St. Boniface, who had made representations on behalf of the Grey Nuns' hospital as a suitable historic site, and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate took pride in claiming his early affinity with the province of Manitoba. Since he abandoned that province it seems he resents the possibility of any service being provided by a reputable representative of the province. If the business in question had gone to someone in Bonavista-Twillingate I suppose he would not have raised an issue.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I would not advise the minister to pursue that line.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I suppose if the business had gone to some of the so called reputable companies that had been associated with this advertising under the former administration he would not have protested. The agency to which he has referred has been in operation for some four years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Since June 21, 1957.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That company is owned and operated by a young man who has been named in this house this morning. He is an outstanding citizen of the city of Brandon, formerly an alderman, who has performed outstanding services for that community. He has handled large contracts in the advertising field, and when the classified advertising business became available in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources it came to that department's attention that this agency was interested, and that individual was asked to apply. The reason I did not know whether there had been any change when I answered the question was that I had not particularly kept in contact with this matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You should always keep in touch with your constituents.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am delighted to know that, following a very thorough investigation by the departmental officials, this young man was considered qualified to handle this particular aspect of advertising.
There were one or two misstatements in the newspaper account on which the hon. member has based his explanations this morning. I


have already referred to the first when I reported that the agency had been in operation for some four years. Mr. Neill, who was formerly associated with Neill's clothing store, has been dissociated from that business for the period he has been operating the advertising agency. There is no cost to the crown in this operation whatsoever. The 15 per cent service charge is paid by the media which receive the advertising. That is the story straight and simple. The hon. member wanted it straight and simple, without any of the interesting and sinister overtones that he imputed, and I am happy to present it in this way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Perhaps I can ask one
question. Before I do so I might point out I made no accusations whatsoever. I suggested nothing sinister. All I did was put on the record of the house what was in two reputable newspapers in Manitoba. I have no information whatsoever about this matter except what I read in the public press. It seemed to me that it was a matter of sufficient interest to the people of Manitoba and to the press- and I might say I have had several letters about it since the matter was first raised here, which would suggest that there is some interest in this matter-to bring up in this committee. But the minister, in his simple, straightforward explanation, has said something that I must answer; or perhaps I should not say this; perhaps charity is called for in a case of this kind. I will just read what Mr. Neill said, according to the Brandon Sun. I point out to the minister that this is according to the Brandon Sun and not the Winnipeg Free Press.
Mr. Neill said he had made no representations to obtain the account.
He said northern affairs minister Dinsdale, who represents Brandon-Souris riding in the commons, had approached him informally about taking the account last December.
I should like to ask the minister whether what Mr. Neill said is the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when I mentioned the fact that this account was available he indicated that he was interested, and that interest was communicated to the officials of the department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Well, I have nothing more to say about this matter, sir, but I should like to ask the minister about another matter that has relationship to Manitoba. Some considerable time ago a motion was passed by this house for the correspondence exchanged between the government of Canada and the government of Manitoba with respect to a very big matter indeed in the affairs of that province. I refer to the Red river floodway, about which, before certain events happened four

years ago, the people who compose the present government, including their leader, made very large promises indeed which there seems to be a good deal of evidence to indicate they are very reluctant to keep. There has been a good deal of pressure in the legislature of Manitoba, and I could read from the Hansard of Manitoba to show this, to have this correspondence produced in that legislature.
On every occasion on which this matter has been brought up the premier of Manitoba has asserted that he could never get the consent of the government of Canada to its production in that house. Over a long period, under the hon. gentleman's predecessor, we had a very similar answer given here, but I must say it is to the credit of the minister that he has taken a rather different attitude toward the matter. He told the house the other day that he had secured the approval of the government of Manitoba to the production of this correspondence. I took it from that that it was the intention of the government to produce it.
I have not had time to check whether the correspondence has been tabled today, but I have checked Votes and Proceedings for the last fews days and there is no record to indicate that it was tabled up until last night. The minister ought to make an effort to make the correspondence available to us at once, during the lunch hour today, so that when his estimates are continued this afternoon we shall have an opportunity to examine the correspondence and ask any questions we wish to about it.
This is a matter of the gravest concern to the government of Manitoba and to the people of that province who have been badly enough treated, as the minister knows well, by the present government in the federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements, and who are in all the greater need of the financial assistance they were led to expect they would get from the present government.
I hope the minister will see that this correspondence is made available to us by 2.30 this afternoon so that it can be examined while his estimates are being discussed. We had in the case of his predecessor, and we have had in the case of some other members of the government, examples of careful efforts to suppress information in this way until the estimates of the department were completed, with the material being produced immediately after, f would not expect the minister to behave in this fashion, and I hope he will accede to my request in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
On this particular point, I have been giving very active consideration to the question of tabling these documents, and I have been following the questioning
90205-6-279J
Supply-Northern Affairs by the hon. member in the house. I have been trying to push the matter forward as quickly as possible. I now discover that because it is a matter for interdepartmental consideration, I shall have to have clearance with the other departments concerned. So far as I am concerned the documents are waiting to be tabled. The hon. member will understand these problems, but this is the cause of the present delay.
With reference to the activities of the present Manitoba provincial administration in this regard, I should like to remind the hon. member that the only answer the previous administration had to this very urgent problem in Manitoba-those of us who lived through the flood of 1950 will never forget the serious threat it was-was, like King Canute, to order the waves to recede. There is positive action going forward, I can assure you, sir and the hon. member, with the Manitoba government at this time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Since it is now one o'clock I hope Your Honour will see me at 2.30, because I should like to make a few observations about the kind of action there has been on this project in the last four years.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, at the time we adjourned for lunch the minister had just made one or two observations which really had nothing to do with the present and which I was rather surprised that this young and dynamic minister should make. When the present minister was appointed I thought we would have an end of these tiresome excuses we get from the government to the effect that because something was not done in the early fifties it should not be done in the sixties. That is the normal pattern of the government. When we ask hon. gentlemen why they have not kept their promises they say that Mr. King did not do that in 1946 or Mr. St. Laurent did not do it in 1952 or Mr. Douglas Campbell did not do it in 1950 as though that had any relation whatsoever to the undertakings these gentlemen opposite gave to the people of Canada, the promissory notes they signed which they refuse to pay. Whatever sins of omission-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What a waste of time. You are just wasting time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman-

Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, when we have to sit here hour after hour and take scoldings from the hon. member such as he is giving us now, it is about time we called him to order because he is not being relevant.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton sat over here when the greatest filibuster in this country in modern times took place, and I do not recall the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton raising any points of order at that time about the fact that the opposition, which was quite considerably larger then than it is now, talked for hours and hours and days and days-with the most tiresome repetition.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: All we are hearing today is purely repetition.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It was anything but repetition to them at that time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is all we are
hearing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Are you attempting to make up for it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Turn the other cheek.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have turned both of them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Order. I think we should come back to the discussion of item No. 279.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I was simply doing what I think Your Honour himself decided was quite within the rules when you were acting for the Speaker in the chair, that if an argument had been introduced by some other hon. member and allowed by the Chair a reply should be allowed. I simply trying to point out to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, who has recently become a member of the cabinet, that if he wants to get ahead in the government of Canada, and heaven knows there is lots of room at the top-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He should not take lessons from you.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As a matter of fact, I have quite a lot of experience in this regard.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You certainly have.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Of course, the hon. member for Calgary South, who belongs to the kindergarten in this house-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
You are its
chairman and you have been for some time.
[Mr. Pickersgill.)

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman, who is very vociferous in the house-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Get to the point.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: -is as usual-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You are fumbling.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: making his speech when someone else is making his. I do not object to that at all but I do not think it is adding up to very much.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What is your subject?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Certainly hon. gentlemen opposite do not like this very much.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You have not said anything yet.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
What I was saying to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris was that if he hoped to get to the top in this government, where there is plenty of room, I might add, I would strongly advise him to deal with the problems of 1961 and 1962 and not to waste his time making excuses for his lack of action and for the lack of action of his colleagues because of something that happened some time during the fifties. I think the people of Canada are growing very weary of that tiresome kind of argument.
Since the hon. gentleman has chosen to pervert the record of the fifties, and since he has said that the people of Winnipeg will never forget what happened in the fifties, may I say that I hope they do not. I hope they never forget about the greatest generosity that has ever been shown to any people in Canada at any time, which was shown by the people of Canada under the leadership of the St. Laurent government in the disaster fund of that time. Complete restitution was made to everybody of their losses and a considerable amount was left over to remain as a disaster fund which has been very helpful to other parts of Canada. I do not believe my right hon. friend Mr. St. Laurent, or any of his colleagues, have any need to be ashamed or have anything to apologize for in connection with what happened with respect to the relief of the suffering caused by the Winnipeg flood or with respect to the study of the problem of preventing such a thing again.
I call to witness no better witness on this subject than the premier of Manitoba who, speaking in the legislature on March 15 of this year, had this to say about what was done after the flood. He was speaking in reply to a member of the opposition and he said:

Do they not know that the engineering aspect of this matter was thoroughly and I think authoritatively, laid down by the investigation of the Red river basin committee that swung into action about 1954.
This is the premier saying the committee swung into action in 1954. The premier is talking about a committee set up jointly by the government of Mr. St. Laurent and the government of Mr. Douglas Campbell. He describes the study as one which was done thoroughly and authoritatively. I continue the quotation:
And they investigated from an engineering standpoint the various methods that were open for the protection of this greater Winnipeg area.
There is no doubt whatever that this was a very thorough engineering investigation. There is no doubt whatever that to the government of Canada and to the government of Manitoba a very serious engineering problem was posed because here was a tremendous expenditure for engineering works that would have no productive advantage whatever. They would be insurance, insurance against a flood happening every so often, perhaps once in half a century and maybe not even that often. Anybody who knows anything about insurance knows that this is a very big and serious problem, to spend tens of millions of dollars to try to avert a contingency that may not arise for a couple of generations. This is the nature of the problem, and it is not an easy problem for anyone to decide.
Hon. gentlemen who are now sitting on the treasury benches thought it was a very easy problem. Of course, they were rather profuse in the promises they made before 1957. They were going to cure everything in the country; they were going to build the Chignecto canal, build a causeway to Prince Edward Island, which they are still studying, and all sorts of other things all over the country. One of the things they were going to do was to make Winnipeg floodproof for all time to come. This year, they finally got the promise into the speech from the throne.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder if I may ask the hon. member a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman tell me what percentage of the money that was contributed to the Winnipeg flood disaster was voluntary and what part of this money came from the then Liberal government?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, I am sure that in the excellent accounts that were kept at that time, which I do not pretend to carry in my head, the hon. gentleman
Supply-Northern Affairs will be able to find that information. According to the rules of the house, even the government is not expected to provide published information in answer to questions. As a member of the opposition-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Then, the hon. member could perhaps tell me-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Perhaps I could finish my answer to this question and then I will answer the hon. gentleman's next question. As a member of the opposition, and not having access to the same research facilities as hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches have, I do not know offhand what the answer is. However, I do not think it has the slightest degree of relevance to the subject we are discussing. Has the hon. member another question he wishes to ask?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think it has some relevance because the hon. member talks about the great amount of money left over from the contributions made by the St, Laurent government. However, I believe that the greatest amount of the money was given voluntarily and the amount that remained was put to other uses because it was voluntary and could be used for other disaster areas in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite right, and that is what I said.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes; if hon. gentlemen will look at the record-I give an undertaking that even if there are some grammatical errors I will not change them, so we will be able to look at it just the way it is being taken down, however lopsided it may be-he will see that what I said was, under the leadership given by the St. Laurent government the people of Canada subscribed in the most generous way I can remember to the relief of this disaster. These contributions were used and there was a great deal of money left over which was set aside as a national disaster fund. Perhaps I could clear up this point for the hon. member for Lisgar. If this money had been contributed out of the treasury, there would not have been any left over, of course. It was because it was in large part a voluntary contribution that some special legislative disposition had to be made. I do not want to denature the record in any way.
What I want to say is, so far as that situation was concerned, so far as the relief of the flood victims was concerned, it was never more complete in the history of Canada than it was in that case. So far as the studies of how to prevent such a situation in the future are concerned, we have Mr. Roblin's

Supply-Northern Affairs own word for it in the provincial legislature this year that the most authoritative and thorough studies were initiated by the previous provincial government and the previous federal government. The suggestion of the minister that there was some neglect by his predecessors in this matter falls completely to the ground. Mr. Roblin has been premier of Manitoba now for three years, and he has certainly been trying to screw some money out of the federal government for this project every year. He is becoming increasingly embarrassed about this as he is about other aspects of his relationships with the federal government.
There are many of us who are beginning to feel rather sorry for Mr. Roblin. I have no doubt that he feels very sorry himself that he ever coined that slogan which I am afraid will never be forgotten, "As Dief did Duff will do." If Mr. Roblin could change it, I think he would say, "As Dief did Duff won't do", if he wanted to make any appeal to the people of Manitoba today. I am not here, of course, to appeal for charity for Mr. Roblin. All I am doing is trying to get this correspondence which has been held up deliberately by this government now for three years, and which the minister gave a very lame excuse for not producing earlier today. I hope he is going to produce it now.
As I say, for three years this correspondence has been held up. Nothing has happened. The legislature has now prorogued for this year, and if anything further is going to be done in co-operation with the federal government there will have to be another session of the legislature for that purpose. As I say, nobody in Manitoba can understand the reason for the delay or what is holding it up. I daresay some of us here with some experience with this government could give the answer. Probably the answer is to be found in a seven letter world starting with "f" and ending with "g". I leave hon. gentlemen opposite to fill in the blanks.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Shall vote 279 carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Just before the vote carries I should like to make some passing references on the subject that has just been discussed at some length by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate. As I explained in my reply this morning, the reason for the delay in tabling the documents has arisen from their interdepartmental nature. Just to demonstrate the desire of my department to be as helpful and co-operative as possible, may I say that I am quite happy to table at this time, if it is the wish of the committee, the documents which come directly under my purview. Where there is interdepartmental involvement, the hon. member will understand that I have


no right to table those documents at this time. However, I shall be happy to let him see the documents which I am sure will ease the problem that has been discussed at some length here today.
It seems to me that we are becoming deeply involved in history during the consideration of these estimates and I feel that it is high time that we should move on to present activities and anticipated future activities. I am not going to pose as an authority on history but there has come to my attention something which I think should be brought before the committee in reference to a historical discussion that took place here last night. It has to do with the highly controversial question as to who first came to Canada's shores. Let me quote from the authorities. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate last night was referred to as the "land-locked mariner from Manitoba". I think that was a more accurate description than the member who made it at that time realized because, on looking into the record of an important voyage of discovery-a record that was made in Sir John Barrow's book entitled "Voyages into the Arctic Region", I find that in 1776 a certain Lieutenant Pickersgill, in command of His Majesty's brig the Lion was directed to proceed to Davis strait for the protection of the British whale fishers-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-and then to continue up the strait and explore the coast of Baffin bay. Barrow records the fact that Pickersgill eventually anchored the Lion in a place to which he gave the name "Musquito Cove".
In case the hon. member's colleague from Essex East should feel neglected, I might also remind the committee that the first of these northern explorers, the privateer Captain Frobisher, bore the Christian name of "Martin". That is the contribution I should like to make to this historical discussion. I could add-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You could add more about Pickersgill.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You could add more about Martin.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Roll in another barrel.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I might say that the descendants of the said Lieutenant Pickersgill have been all at sea ever since.
We have a little bit more time at our disposal at the moment and perhaps, because it seems to be the wish of the members of the committee, I might give answers to some of the specific questions that were raised last evening.

I would reply to the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg and inform him that one of the subjects he raised, namely the possibility of the blockhouse hill in his constituency being recognized as a historic site, will be considered on the May agenda of the national historic sites and monuments board.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River inquired about progress on the civic centre at Banff national park. X am happy to inform him-and unfortunately he is not in the chamber-that tenders have been asked for in connection with this project and we hope that it will be under way just as quickly as possible. He also inquired whether it was established policy in national parks to assist in the construction of centres of this kind. I should merely like to remind him that Banff is almost a unique community in the national parks system. In fact, so far as I know, there are only two such communities where there is all year round residence. Therefore, this instance might be regarded as almost unique.
The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria made reference to Englishtown. I can assure him that this question will be on the May agenda of the historic sites and monuments board. He will also be interested to know that the HD4 Hydrofoil will be provided with a suitable shelter in the fiscal year 1962-63 according to present plans.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare brought to the attention of the committee some interesting recommendations. I think he is aware of the fact that there is at Yarmouth already a monument to shipbuilding.
I should like to refer back to one matter in particular referred to by the hon. member for Athabasca. I refer to the question of representation by the R.C.M.P. on the Northwest Territories council. I assure him that the contribution made by the R.C.M.P. to the development of the north down through the years is fully recognized by the department of northern affairs. Any change in the membership of the Northwest Territories council is merely in line with the policy to proceed to an autonomous position in the territories just as quickly as circumstances allow. We like to feel that the territories are independent in their governmental function as far as is possible under the present arrangement.
For some number of years on the Northwest Territories council, where there were formerly representatives from the various departments of government, we have been and are now following the policy of bringing in private citizens. In fact, now there are elected members as well as appointed representatives. The Department of National Defence is no longer represented. Neither is there direct representation from the R.C.M.P.
Supply-Northern Affairs However, let me repeat that the continuing contribution of the R.C.M.P. is full recognized.
The hon. member for Athabasca will also be interested to know that the road construction program in Wood Buffalo national park is proceeding according to schedule. By next year we shall have completed the road from Fort Smith through to the western boundary of Wood Buffalo national park. All that will remain for the continuous highway between Vermilion and Fort Smith will be a road built by the provincial government to the boundary of the park. I might also add that the total cost of this project will be $2,340,000.
Those are some specific answers to specific questions. The committee is in a congenial mood this afternoon and I am sure we can proceed to consider further items of the estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I understood the minister to say that some of the applications for preserving historic sites in Canada are to be dealt with next month. If that is the case, I wonder whether the minister would take a personal look at the old stone house in Sault Ste. Marie and see whether something could not be done to preserve that building as a historic site. It was built in 1812 or 1814 and it is, I believe, the oldest stone building in Ontario north of Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As the hon. member has suggested, the historic sites and monuments board will be meeting toward the end of the present month. I shall be happy to look into this question but I should like to remind the hon. member that the basic criterion for having any historic site considered as a national historic site is, of course, the national aspect. It must have national significance. There are many other historic sites which deserve to be commemorated and such commemoration has been undertaken in the past, sometimes by provincial governments and at other times by local bodies. Subject to that reservation I shall be happy to look into the matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On several occasions I have raised the question of the proposed United States legislation regarding duty free goods which United States citizens are to be allowed to take back from Canada. I wonder if the minister has anything to say in this regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member that I have been following this question very closely since it first came under discussion in the house. As he is no doubt aware, the matter is before congress at the present time and to make certain that Canada's viewpoint on this question is in no way misunderstood by the legislators in the United

Supply-Northern Affairs States, I once again, only recently, pointed out through our Department of External Affairs the importance of this subject to Canada and in particular to the Canadian tourist industry.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Could I ask the minister to take a good look at the posibility of having Nellie McClung's home in the town of Mani-tou, Manitoba made a historic site? This great Canadian woman lived in this house which has been kept in a good state of preservation during the years when she did much of her writing and it seems to me the people of Manitoba would be very pleased if the minister would have this considered as a historic site.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Since the hon. member for Lisgar is very anxious to commemorate the home of one leading Liberal in Manitoba, may I ask if he would also suggest that the home of the Hon. Thomas Greenaway in Crystal City should also be considered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I did not know it was in order to direct such a question to an ordinary backbencher but I would think that though Mr. Thomas Greenaway is probably one of our better known Manitoba citizens his work is hardly of such a national nature that his home should be enshrined as a national historic site. I would suggest, however, that the hon. member might perhaps consider the home of the Hon. Robert Rogers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is it still there?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is a tolerance and liberality about the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that I wish I could share, but I cannot reach it. He put on the record his case from the Brandon Sun and the Winnipeg Free Press and, frankly he is so tolerant I cannot understand his reasoning. I did not know anything about the case before he put it so clearly and it seems to me the minister's answers were inadequate.
I should like to remind the minister that several years ago we had a hassle over the Riding Mountain national park situation. I can remember that there were charges and counter-charges of patronage, and the discussion did not simmer down until the hon. member for Brandon-Souris came in with his soft, susurrus voice and settled it all; we really did not believe that patronage could rear its ugly head at the park if the hon. member had any connection with the affair.
I do not think that the passage of these estimates has been marked, so far, with blood and fire, but I might ask the minister to give us some further explanations. I will put a few direct questions to him. Was Mr. Neill a member of his party organization at


any time? Was Mr. Neill by any chance a census enumerator? Did Mr. Neill have any great interest in advertising before? I tried looking through directories of firms in the west-a very inadequate source to look at, I admit-but I could not find any indication that this man had been long in the business. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is not suspicious at all, but for me there is something coincidental about this business starting up in 1957 in relation to this contract and the minister taking over his portfolio. If the minister were to tell me point blank that Conservatives rank first'-and we had some indication of this in connection with the census matter-that would be fine, but I did not realize this applied to such things as advertising contracts.
There is no point in the minister giving to me the same answer he gave to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate because Cockfield Brown means nought to me though it may mean a great deal to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I believe there is a C.C.F. advertising concern out in Regina but whether it has had any jobs I cannot say. I do not want it to have this job. I would simply like to know if it is a fact that we have here a Conservative who, on the government coming into power, became an advertising agent; and then, when the present minister became minister of northern affairs -an old hometown boy and all that-he was given this contract. Is it as simple as that? Was the contract put out to tender? Did a number of Conservatives bid for it? For all I know there may be a whole bunch of Conservative advertising men in Brandon. I think the minister should give us a more detailed explanation because I am just not as tolerant and liberal today as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am sorry that my learned friend did not grasp the full import of the reply I gave to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I thought I had made a complete explanation. The hon. member has gone back into history with reference to Riding Mountain national park and I assure him the reason that particular subject ceased to come under discussion in the house was because the difficulty was straightened out, as he well knows.
Regarding the advertising accounts, I understand that tenders are not involved in the advertising accounts of government departments, particularly with reference to the classified type which has come under discussion today. I would reiterate that it is the publicity media, whether it be the press, magazines, radio, or television, which pays

the service charge on these particular advertisement items. There is no charge to the crown whatsoever.
So far as the qualifications of the manager of the Neill Advertising Agency in Brandon is concerned, I would repeat that he is a very reputable businessman who, at a remarkably young age, has shown considerable enterprise not only in the business world but also in public service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And in the political world.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He has been active in the past in the Young Progressive Conservatives' Association, which I think demonstrates he is a man of considerable discernment and wisdom. While checking further regarding his credentials'-this is something I did not know before-I found he is accredited to a reputable advertising agency in Canada.
