Hon. gentlemen who are now sitting on the treasury benches thought it was a very easy problem. Of course, they were rather profuse in the promises they made before 1957. They were going to cure everything in the country; they were going to build the Chignecto canal, build a causeway to Prince Edward Island, which they are still studying, and all sorts of other things all over the country. One of the things they were going to do was to make Winnipeg floodproof for all time to come. This year, they finally got the promise into the speech from the throne.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder if I may ask the hon. member a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman tell me what percentage of the money that was contributed to the Winnipeg flood disaster was voluntary and what part of this money came from the then Liberal government?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, I am sure that in the excellent accounts that were kept at that time, which I do not pretend to carry in my head, the hon. gentleman
Supply-Northern Affairs will be able to find that information. According to the rules of the house, even the government is not expected to provide published information in answer to questions. As a member of the opposition-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Then, the hon. member could perhaps tell me-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Perhaps I could finish my answer to this question and then I will answer the hon. gentleman's next question. As a member of the opposition, and not having access to the same research facilities as hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches have, I do not know offhand what the answer is. However, I do not think it has the slightest degree of relevance to the subject we are discussing. Has the hon. member another question he wishes to ask?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think it has some relevance because the hon. member talks about the great amount of money left over from the contributions made by the St, Laurent government. However, I believe that the greatest amount of the money was given voluntarily and the amount that remained was put to other uses because it was voluntary and could be used for other disaster areas in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite right, and that is what I said.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes; if hon. gentlemen will look at the record-I give an undertaking that even if there are some grammatical errors I will not change them, so we will be able to look at it just the way it is being taken down, however lopsided it may be-he will see that what I said was, under the leadership given by the St. Laurent government the people of Canada subscribed in the most generous way I can remember to the relief of this disaster. These contributions were used and there was a great deal of money left over which was set aside as a national disaster fund. Perhaps I could clear up this point for the hon. member for Lisgar. If this money had been contributed out of the treasury, there would not have been any left over, of course. It was because it was in large part a voluntary contribution that some special legislative disposition had to be made. I do not want to denature the record in any way.
What I want to say is, so far as that situation was concerned, so far as the relief of the flood victims was concerned, it was never more complete in the history of Canada than it was in that case. So far as the studies of how to prevent such a situation in the future are concerned, we have Mr. Roblin's

Supply-Northern Affairs own word for it in the provincial legislature this year that the most authoritative and thorough studies were initiated by the previous provincial government and the previous federal government. The suggestion of the minister that there was some neglect by his predecessors in this matter falls completely to the ground. Mr. Roblin has been premier of Manitoba now for three years, and he has certainly been trying to screw some money out of the federal government for this project every year. He is becoming increasingly embarrassed about this as he is about other aspects of his relationships with the federal government.
There are many of us who are beginning to feel rather sorry for Mr. Roblin. I have no doubt that he feels very sorry himself that he ever coined that slogan which I am afraid will never be forgotten, "As Dief did Duff will do." If Mr. Roblin could change it, I think he would say, "As Dief did Duff won't do", if he wanted to make any appeal to the people of Manitoba today. I am not here, of course, to appeal for charity for Mr. Roblin. All I am doing is trying to get this correspondence which has been held up deliberately by this government now for three years, and which the minister gave a very lame excuse for not producing earlier today. I hope he is going to produce it now.
As I say, for three years this correspondence has been held up. Nothing has happened. The legislature has now prorogued for this year, and if anything further is going to be done in co-operation with the federal government there will have to be another session of the legislature for that purpose. As I say, nobody in Manitoba can understand the reason for the delay or what is holding it up. I daresay some of us here with some experience with this government could give the answer. Probably the answer is to be found in a seven letter world starting with "f" and ending with "g". I leave hon. gentlemen opposite to fill in the blanks.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Shall vote 279 carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Just before the vote carries I should like to make some passing references on the subject that has just been discussed at some length by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate. As I explained in my reply this morning, the reason for the delay in tabling the documents has arisen from their interdepartmental nature. Just to demonstrate the desire of my department to be as helpful and co-operative as possible, may I say that I am quite happy to table at this time, if it is the wish of the committee, the documents which come directly under my purview. Where there is interdepartmental involvement, the hon. member will understand that I have


no right to table those documents at this time. However, I shall be happy to let him see the documents which I am sure will ease the problem that has been discussed at some length here today.
It seems to me that we are becoming deeply involved in history during the consideration of these estimates and I feel that it is high time that we should move on to present activities and anticipated future activities. I am not going to pose as an authority on history but there has come to my attention something which I think should be brought before the committee in reference to a historical discussion that took place here last night. It has to do with the highly controversial question as to who first came to Canada's shores. Let me quote from the authorities. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate last night was referred to as the "land-locked mariner from Manitoba". I think that was a more accurate description than the member who made it at that time realized because, on looking into the record of an important voyage of discovery-a record that was made in Sir John Barrow's book entitled "Voyages into the Arctic Region", I find that in 1776 a certain Lieutenant Pickersgill, in command of His Majesty's brig the Lion was directed to proceed to Davis strait for the protection of the British whale fishers-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-and then to continue up the strait and explore the coast of Baffin bay. Barrow records the fact that Pickersgill eventually anchored the Lion in a place to which he gave the name "Musquito Cove".
In case the hon. member's colleague from Essex East should feel neglected, I might also remind the committee that the first of these northern explorers, the privateer Captain Frobisher, bore the Christian name of "Martin". That is the contribution I should like to make to this historical discussion. I could add-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You could add more about Pickersgill.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You could add more about Martin.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Roll in another barrel.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I might say that the descendants of the said Lieutenant Pickersgill have been all at sea ever since.
We have a little bit more time at our disposal at the moment and perhaps, because it seems to be the wish of the members of the committee, I might give answers to some of the specific questions that were raised last evening.

I would reply to the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg and inform him that one of the subjects he raised, namely the possibility of the blockhouse hill in his constituency being recognized as a historic site, will be considered on the May agenda of the national historic sites and monuments board.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River inquired about progress on the civic centre at Banff national park. X am happy to inform him-and unfortunately he is not in the chamber-that tenders have been asked for in connection with this project and we hope that it will be under way just as quickly as possible. He also inquired whether it was established policy in national parks to assist in the construction of centres of this kind. I should merely like to remind him that Banff is almost a unique community in the national parks system. In fact, so far as I know, there are only two such communities where there is all year round residence. Therefore, this instance might be regarded as almost unique.
The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria made reference to Englishtown. I can assure him that this question will be on the May agenda of the historic sites and monuments board. He will also be interested to know that the HD4 Hydrofoil will be provided with a suitable shelter in the fiscal year 1962-63 according to present plans.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare brought to the attention of the committee some interesting recommendations. I think he is aware of the fact that there is at Yarmouth already a monument to shipbuilding.
I should like to refer back to one matter in particular referred to by the hon. member for Athabasca. I refer to the question of representation by the R.C.M.P. on the Northwest Territories council. I assure him that the contribution made by the R.C.M.P. to the development of the north down through the years is fully recognized by the department of northern affairs. Any change in the membership of the Northwest Territories council is merely in line with the policy to proceed to an autonomous position in the territories just as quickly as circumstances allow. We like to feel that the territories are independent in their governmental function as far as is possible under the present arrangement.
For some number of years on the Northwest Territories council, where there were formerly representatives from the various departments of government, we have been and are now following the policy of bringing in private citizens. In fact, now there are elected members as well as appointed representatives. The Department of National Defence is no longer represented. Neither is there direct representation from the R.C.M.P.
Supply-Northern Affairs However, let me repeat that the continuing contribution of the R.C.M.P. is full recognized.
The hon. member for Athabasca will also be interested to know that the road construction program in Wood Buffalo national park is proceeding according to schedule. By next year we shall have completed the road from Fort Smith through to the western boundary of Wood Buffalo national park. All that will remain for the continuous highway between Vermilion and Fort Smith will be a road built by the provincial government to the boundary of the park. I might also add that the total cost of this project will be $2,340,000.
Those are some specific answers to specific questions. The committee is in a congenial mood this afternoon and I am sure we can proceed to consider further items of the estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I understood the minister to say that some of the applications for preserving historic sites in Canada are to be dealt with next month. If that is the case, I wonder whether the minister would take a personal look at the old stone house in Sault Ste. Marie and see whether something could not be done to preserve that building as a historic site. It was built in 1812 or 1814 and it is, I believe, the oldest stone building in Ontario north of Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As the hon. member has suggested, the historic sites and monuments board will be meeting toward the end of the present month. I shall be happy to look into this question but I should like to remind the hon. member that the basic criterion for having any historic site considered as a national historic site is, of course, the national aspect. It must have national significance. There are many other historic sites which deserve to be commemorated and such commemoration has been undertaken in the past, sometimes by provincial governments and at other times by local bodies. Subject to that reservation I shall be happy to look into the matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On several occasions I have raised the question of the proposed United States legislation regarding duty free goods which United States citizens are to be allowed to take back from Canada. I wonder if the minister has anything to say in this regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member that I have been following this question very closely since it first came under discussion in the house. As he is no doubt aware, the matter is before congress at the present time and to make certain that Canada's viewpoint on this question is in no way misunderstood by the legislators in the United

Supply-Northern Affairs States, I once again, only recently, pointed out through our Department of External Affairs the importance of this subject to Canada and in particular to the Canadian tourist industry.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Could I ask the minister to take a good look at the posibility of having Nellie McClung's home in the town of Mani-tou, Manitoba made a historic site? This great Canadian woman lived in this house which has been kept in a good state of preservation during the years when she did much of her writing and it seems to me the people of Manitoba would be very pleased if the minister would have this considered as a historic site.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Since the hon. member for Lisgar is very anxious to commemorate the home of one leading Liberal in Manitoba, may I ask if he would also suggest that the home of the Hon. Thomas Greenaway in Crystal City should also be considered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I did not know it was in order to direct such a question to an ordinary backbencher but I would think that though Mr. Thomas Greenaway is probably one of our better known Manitoba citizens his work is hardly of such a national nature that his home should be enshrined as a national historic site. I would suggest, however, that the hon. member might perhaps consider the home of the Hon. Robert Rogers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is it still there?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is a tolerance and liberality about the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that I wish I could share, but I cannot reach it. He put on the record his case from the Brandon Sun and the Winnipeg Free Press and, frankly he is so tolerant I cannot understand his reasoning. I did not know anything about the case before he put it so clearly and it seems to me the minister's answers were inadequate.
I should like to remind the minister that several years ago we had a hassle over the Riding Mountain national park situation. I can remember that there were charges and counter-charges of patronage, and the discussion did not simmer down until the hon. member for Brandon-Souris came in with his soft, susurrus voice and settled it all; we really did not believe that patronage could rear its ugly head at the park if the hon. member had any connection with the affair.
I do not think that the passage of these estimates has been marked, so far, with blood and fire, but I might ask the minister to give us some further explanations. I will put a few direct questions to him. Was Mr. Neill a member of his party organization at


any time? Was Mr. Neill by any chance a census enumerator? Did Mr. Neill have any great interest in advertising before? I tried looking through directories of firms in the west-a very inadequate source to look at, I admit-but I could not find any indication that this man had been long in the business. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is not suspicious at all, but for me there is something coincidental about this business starting up in 1957 in relation to this contract and the minister taking over his portfolio. If the minister were to tell me point blank that Conservatives rank first'-and we had some indication of this in connection with the census matter-that would be fine, but I did not realize this applied to such things as advertising contracts.
There is no point in the minister giving to me the same answer he gave to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate because Cockfield Brown means nought to me though it may mean a great deal to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I believe there is a C.C.F. advertising concern out in Regina but whether it has had any jobs I cannot say. I do not want it to have this job. I would simply like to know if it is a fact that we have here a Conservative who, on the government coming into power, became an advertising agent; and then, when the present minister became minister of northern affairs -an old hometown boy and all that-he was given this contract. Is it as simple as that? Was the contract put out to tender? Did a number of Conservatives bid for it? For all I know there may be a whole bunch of Conservative advertising men in Brandon. I think the minister should give us a more detailed explanation because I am just not as tolerant and liberal today as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am sorry that my learned friend did not grasp the full import of the reply I gave to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I thought I had made a complete explanation. The hon. member has gone back into history with reference to Riding Mountain national park and I assure him the reason that particular subject ceased to come under discussion in the house was because the difficulty was straightened out, as he well knows.
Regarding the advertising accounts, I understand that tenders are not involved in the advertising accounts of government departments, particularly with reference to the classified type which has come under discussion today. I would reiterate that it is the publicity media, whether it be the press, magazines, radio, or television, which pays

the service charge on these particular advertisement items. There is no charge to the crown whatsoever.
So far as the qualifications of the manager of the Neill Advertising Agency in Brandon is concerned, I would repeat that he is a very reputable businessman who, at a remarkably young age, has shown considerable enterprise not only in the business world but also in public service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And in the political world.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He has been active in the past in the Young Progressive Conservatives' Association, which I think demonstrates he is a man of considerable discernment and wisdom. While checking further regarding his credentials'-this is something I did not know before-I found he is accredited to a reputable advertising agency in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am pleased to find this candour at last. It is of assistance. I think the people of Canada will be pleased to know that it is a help to be a young Conservative or a Progressive Conservative if it is desired to acquire these advertising contracts. These are facts of life which are sometimes denied. I am not complaining about this at all but now we know that if one wants an advertising contract with the minister's department it helps if one is a Conservative.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out that Mr. Neill's advertising agency is the only one in the city of Brandon, and if there were an advertising agency operated by a C.C.F. supporter we would be pleased to consider him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
What advantage does the city of Brandon have which flows from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources? I am sure the minister made his offer in respect of all of Canada, but does he intend that all those individuals should line up to see him about an advertising agency? There is an advertising agency in Port Arthur which is run by a Conservative, and I am wondering whether he would be a fair candidate. I suggest that we should let him know about this situation.
I would like to ask the minister a question about something else. I realize he is just getting into his job, and I am sure he is reviewing these things, but the Massey commission made a number of recommendations in relation to certain agencies under the control of the minister's department. I wonder whether the minister would care to comment regarding the steps which have been taken to implement these recommendations, and perhaps comment about those which he does not intend to implement at all. I am
Supply-Northern Affairs not interested in the war museum particularly but much more in regard to situations such as the one discovered in Newfoundland by Mr. Smallwood who said the federal government should be stopped from shanghaiing relics for monuments from the sacred soil of Newfoundland. I believe the Massey commission made certain recommendations in regard to both national relics and monuments, and those bearing a relationship to the United States, and I would like to know what the minister has done in this regard. As far as I am aware there has been no legislation introduced in this house bearing on that subject.
I would also like to ask the minister about the part French Canadians play in the structure of the national museum? We all remember the unfortunate affair involving the separation of Dr. Rousseau. I understand he is now over in Europe carrying out some kind of task. The minister is probably aware that Dr. Rousseau was separated from his rather important job in the department, and I am wondering what has been done in this regard. The Prime Minister is always talking about our bicultural and bilingual country, but it is sometimes difficult to appreciate that our French Canadian representatives have a share in the upper management of these particularly cultural assets, such as the national museum. I wonder whether the minister could let us know what he is doing in regard to seeing that this balance is redressed.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I see my hon. friend is continuing to play his role as a pedagogue in assigning certain research programs to me this afternoon. I assure him I am vitally interested in the recommendations of the Massey commission with respect to many matters, particularly those which come within the purview of my department.
He will remember that one of the recommendations had to do with the protection of archaeological sites in Canada, and the artifacts from those sites. Up until quite recently many of these irreplaceable archaeological treasures had been lost to Canada by reason of uncontrolled development and exploitation. We have been very active in the protection of these sites, mainly through encouragement in the training of Canadian anthropologists. This is something which cannot be resolved overnight by this method; that is, by ensuring that there are a sufficient number of qualified Canadian professional personnel to take care of this important work.
One of the difficulties in finding suitable bilingual staff for our museums arises from the fact we do not have a sufficiently large number of Canadians with the necessary professional training who possess bilingual

Supply-Northern Affairs ability. I am happy to say that we have made certain progress in this regard. The national museum staff includes 21 members who speak French fluently, of whom four are professional scientists. A number of other staff members have a working knowledge of the French language, but great difficulty has been found in filling some of the highly specialized positions at the museum with staff who are bilingual and it has been necessary in some cases to find applicants from outside Canada. We are quite confident that, with the encouragement which has been given to training Canadians, this difficulty will be resolved within a comparatively short time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the minister a few questions in regard to the item covering museums. I would like to know whether Dr. Rousseau has been replaced by a French speaking employee at the museum.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there has been no permanent replacement found as yet. This is the human history side of the museum's activities and the director of the museum, Dr. Russell, is serving in an acting capacity until such time as a suitable candidate is found.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Do I understand from the minister's remarks that he expects to choose a French speaking candidate for this position?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we are seeking very diligently for the right sort of candidate, and if we find a French speaking candidate with the necessary qualifications we shall be happy to consider him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question in relation to national parks, and the matter of skiing. I would like to know what representations have been made in the past by the Canadian ski patrol association in respect of extending its activities into national park areas or, if not extending their activities into that field, perhaps in helping to standardize safety patrol procedures which may be carried out at present by national parks personnel.
In saying this I am not suggesting any criticism of what the parks may be doing- I do not know what they are doing-but I should like to know whether in this rather fairly rapidly growing safety movement in the field of skiing, and skiing is the fastest growing sport we have that relates to tourism, there is any liaison established between the parks and the skiing patrol association and, of course, the C.A.S.A. itself, which is in a sense the parent organization of the Canadian ski patrol.


I have one last question in relation to historic sites and monuments that I should like to put to the minister. A group of the citizens of Fort William have become enthusiastic about re-creating the old Fort William. A committee has been organized, I think it is called the committee to restore the old fort, and it has sent letters to a number of people, including the members for Fort William and Port Arthur and also the Prime Minister. Having regard to our present budgetary position, 1 was somewhat amazed at the very optimistic reply the Prime Minister gave to this association, indicating that there is an excellent chance that government support of a very substantial kind will be available to renovate this fort or to create the old fort anew. Since the scale of expenditure to recreate the fort would be in the nature of several hundred thousand dollars and since, as I said, the Prime Minister was, in the letter I read, fairly optimistic about it, can the minister indicate whether this whole question has been brought to the attention of his department, and whether the Fort William fort is one of the projects that is being appraised or analysed at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am very pleased to see the interest of the hon. member in the matter of skiing development in our national parks. Obviously he has caught the enthusiasm of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this respect. I do not know whether he himself is personally a skier, but I can assure him that one of the activities we regard as highly suitable to the fundamental purpose of the national parks is that of winter skiing. Boating, hiking, swimming, and all those activities which are closely associated with the enjoyment of nature are the type of recreational activities we like to encourage.
In the mountain parks, of course, the skiing development has gone on much more rapidly than in other areas. I am happy to inform the hon. member that in Riding Mountain national park there is a ski site under development at the present time. I think perhaps there is a slight misunderstanding. The national parks branch as such does not actually participate in the skiing operation itself. It provides the site and develops it and then it is turned over to private enterprise to operate as a recreational feature.
In regard to the safety patrol group, I can assure the hon. member also that wherever there is skiing activity in our national parks the skiers themselves see to it that they have close liaison with the ski patrol.
With respect to the other question, the old Fort William site has been very thoroughly examined and investigated by the historic

sites and monument board. As the hon. member knows, this board is made up of outstanding historians in Canada, including men of the stature of Dr. Creighton. They are selected to advise the government on the historic facts surrounding those various sites.
The difficulty in connection with Fort William-and I believe this information has been communicated to the hon. member-arises from the fact that the original site is no longer available. We cannot have the historic site, of course, if it is no longer available. That has been the fundamental difficulty in connection with the development of this historic site.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have one further question to ask the minister. It relates to a private member's public bill on the order paper at the present time. Since the minister heads the department responsible for this whole question of historic sites and monuments, I wonder whether he has given any consideration to helping the hon. member for Brantford, or helping to sponsor as a government measure, relating to the idea of creating a national holiday of the birthday anniversary of Sir John A. Macdonald? Has any consideration been given to that matter by this particular committee? I know it is an abstract thing rather than something concrete, but after all the creation of a day every year as an annual holiday would be a monument, I am sure the minister would agree. I should like to know whether he has given any consideration to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, Mr. Chairman, although my department ranges far and wide, and although the hon. member does not think I do anything, let me say that despite the fact that we are a busy department, this is one function that does not come under my purview. The question that he has raised would be regarded more as a historic institution than a historic site. I mean that in a sociological sense, because it is certainly true that Sir John A. as the founder of this nation, as the man who first established the national policy which made this country great, should be commemorated in this way. The present government is carrying on this national policy and moving Canada forward from strength to strength and I am sure we appreciate the hon. member's recognition of the fact.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If we can get back once again into the twentieth century, sir, I should like to ask the minister whether Fort Rodd in Victoria has been taken over by the historic sites and monuments board? Can he tell me at the same time on what date this request was first made or the matter was first
Supply-Northern Affairs brought to the attention of the historic sites and monuments board, and on what date they made their decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have not the specific dates referred to by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He himself implied just a few moments ago in a reply that he did not carry these detailed statistics around in his head, and neither do I. But I do assure him that Fort Rodd has been taken over by the historic sites and monuments board, and it has been recognized by that board as a national historic site.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Perhaps during the course of the passage of the estimates the minister can get the information and give me the date on which the matter was first brought to the attention of the historic sites and monuments board and the date on which the decision was made. I should really like to have that information later on but I am not pressing for it immediately.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have before me some figures on several items of the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. One of them relates to travelling and removals. The figures in 1957 were $625,854. The estimate for this year is twice that, $1,273,968. I should like the minister to tell us if he will the reason for this and also for the increase in telephones and telegraphs which in 1957 amounted to $40,869. The figures are over three times that in the estimates for 1961-62, $127,811.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as was pointed out several times during the course of this discussion, there has been a great increase in activity in the north during the past two years, and the increase in expenditures to which the hon. member has referred is related directly to this tremendous upsurge of northern development. Transportation is one of the major difficulties in northern Canada, as the hon. member will appreciate. Northern Canada constitutes 40 per cent of our total land area; it is rich in minerals and resources of all kinds, including human resources. This increased cost is merely a reflection of the increased activity and the same applies, of course, to the cost of telephones, telegrams and so on. There was a time not long ago when such communication was quite impossible, and this is all evidence of the tremendous development taking place in the north.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have had a few minutes to look at this correspondence with the Manitoba government which the minister explained was incomplete, although I must say I have not been able to peruse it very carefully. I think the minister owes
4424	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs the committee a better explanation of the delay of the government in dealing with the Winnipeg floodway than simply to read about Lieutenant Richard Pickersgill who went to Baffin land in the late eighteenth century. I have here, for example, a letter written by Mr. Roblin, the premier of Manitoba, on February 4, 1960; not 1961, but 1960. The letter was addressed to the minister's predecessor, of course, who may have been absorbed with visions at that time that did not embrace the Red river. The second paragraph reads as follows:
I am naturally pleased to have this advice-
The advice referred to was that contained in the previous paragraph, that a member of the water resources branch had been appointed to consult with the officials of Manitoba.
-and I hope that the necessary approval will be forthcoming in time to allow us to take advantage of the coming construction season.
That was the construction season of 1960. February 4, 1960 happened to be the same day, of course, that the Minister of Labour was on the air on "The Nation's Business" telling us that the recession was over, and it may be that in February 1960 the government did not think it was important to have work in Manitoba in the summer of 1960. However, before the summer of 1960 was over even the most obtuse members of the government must have been convinced that any project that would supply more work would have been a useful thing to undertake. But Mr. Roblin, of course, did not get any construction under way. He did not get any approvals in 1960.
Then there are some other bits and pieces of correspondence involving other departments that would have to be fitted into the jigsaw puzzle but those departments have not yet seen lit to bring down their correspondence. However, I have here a letter which it is not possible for me to understand fully because the letter in reply to which this letter is written to the present minister by the minister of agriculure of Manitoba is not here. The letter is dated January 3, 1961, and it makes certain proposals with respect to getting on with the floodway. I gather that the minister of agriculture of Manitoba has ministerial responsibility for this project which the Manitoba government seems to want to carry out but in which the federal government seems very reluctant to take any part notwithstanding its promises of 1957 and 1958. Let me read the last paragraph of Mr. Hutton's pathetic appeal in January of 1961 when unemployment had reached the highest peak it had reached since the thirties. Mr. Hutton wrote as follows:


I would request your early consideration of the above proposal, your advice as to whether it meets your approval and if so, assurance that your government would be prepared to include the cost of the above services as part of the shareable costs of the floodway project.
I draw attention to these words, and point out this is from a Tory government, a very friendly government, one supposes. This was in January of this year.
I am sure you realize that it is imperative that this project get under way as quickly as possible but that before doing so the very considerable amount of planning and design work must be undertaken. Your earliest possible consideration and advice in respect to this matter would therefore be appreciated.
That was on January 3 of this year. I look at the calendar and see it is the 5th of May. The record is not quite equal to that of the Minister of Finance with respect to depressed areas but very nearly so. Four months have gone by and there has been no answer. I assume there has been no answer because if there had been one I assume it would have been produced with the correspondence. If this is the way the government treats a friendly Tory government, you can imagine the way it treats governments that do not have the advantage of having in them young Conservatives, as the hon. member for Port Arthur pointed out. I think the minister should tell us what has happened with respect to this floodway.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Are you going to run in Manitoba in the next election?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is too bad, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate ever forsook Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Not too bad for Manitoba though.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We would have a wonderful advocate had he not shaken the dust of that province from his feet and sought fame and fortune in eastern Canada. In reading the letter he has been rather selective.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I read just the last paragraph and I said so.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think that reading just the last paragraph did not give the full purport of the document. Actually what the minister of agriculture of Manitoba was discussing was the idea of setting up a joint committee to consider the engineering problems with respect to the floodway development. I am happy to assure the hon. member that that committee is operating and busily engaged in working on the necessary details.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would the minister tell us what the division of costs is going to be for this project?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As I have intimated when questioned on this point on earlier occasions, this is a subject that is under negotiation and it is one of the reserved items in the documents.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The Manitoba government cannot proceed unless they do what Mr. Rob-lin, I thought rather foolishly, threatened to do on one occasion, pay for it themselves. He did not know with whom he was dealing when he made that remark, and I suspect it was a bad day for Manitoba when he made it. The question of the division of costs has been discussed for two years. It has been discussed in the legislature and, judging from the debates which I have read and some of which I had in my hand a few moments ago but sent to the Hansard office, Mr. Roblin has been red-faced and embarrassed over this matter because his friends were not coming across. It seems to me that surely this is not such an insuperable problem. Surely the government can make up its mind about a question of this sort if indeed it ever intends to do anything about it, which a lot of us suspect it does not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is one point about which I have not asked the minister. I do not think it is a particularly delicate one, but several months ago I noticed in the Manchester Guardian a news story to the effect that the bishop of the Arctic was in Britain recruiting young men in particular to work in the Arctic. I am sorry I do not have the quotation here. I could not find it in my file. However, I think it is fair to say that the gist of it was that it was extremely difficult to obtain within Canada itself the kind of people to carry on the many necessary chores, not particularly in religious work, although that was involved, but in teaching and other fields. Can the minister indicate to me as someone who does not know very much about the matter whether it is a fact that the Anglican schools are having great difficulty in securing teachers and that they have to recruit from outside of Canada in order to keep the facilities operating?
I should like to know also, if this should be the case, if these schools in the north run by the Anglican church are being staffed by people from England? Is any consideration being given to giving some kind of assistance so that Canadian teachers can be put in these schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In reply to this question I shall have to correct a misunderstanding. The schools in the Arctic are federal schools; they are not church schools as such. The
Supply-Northern Affairs churches have the responsibility of operating the residential hostels, which are a very important adjunct to our school operation because of the distances involved. They are federal government schools, and are operated as such.
In so far as the problem of staffing the schools in the north is concerned, I shall be quite frank and say there is some difficulty in getting suitable candidates as teachers. It was because of this situation that I suggested the hon. member might be interested in going north. I assure him, in reply to what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said, that should he indicate his desire to go north his application would be duly processed by the civil service. It is done in that manner so that we can get the best possible candidates.
While it is difficult to get suitable candidates, I might also add that I am informed each and every teacher in the federal schools in the Arctic is a Canadian. I am very happy to inform the committee that with the growing interest in the north, more and more of our young men and young women are willing to come forward and pioneer in this new frontier.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In so far as this point is concerned, one of the reasons for my misunderstanding was probably the explanation the minister gave some time ago in connection with the difficulties of teaching French in northern Quebec and Labrador. The minister's answer seemed to stress the Anglican religion of the people, and I assumed this meant the framework of the school system still had a religious bias or religious foundation. I quite clearly gained the impression from the reported remarks of the bishop of the Arctic that he was recruiting for more than just members of the clergy to go into the north.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I can assure the hon. member that he was recruiting missionaries for work in the north. It is unfortunate the wrong impression was left or created by the reply to the question the other morning. The denominational aspects in our Arctic schools enter in in relation to the selection of teachers. Where there is a greater percentage of Anglican adherents, the teacher is from the Anglican faith. Where there is a substantial majority of the Roman Catholic faith, the teacher is of the Roman Catholic faith.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I should like to ask the
minister to clarify his statement. The minister is talking about schools in the Arctic. The question was asked in relation to Eskimo schools in the province of Quebec. The minister is not suggesting that his department is running schools in the province of Quebec?

Supply-Northern Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. If the hon. gentleman will examine his map of Canada, he will find there is an area of the Arctic in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is not my question at all. I asked if the department of northern affairs is conducting any schools in the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes. It has been pointed out to me, Mr. Chairman, that there are eleven Eskimo schools operated by the department of northern affairs in northern Quebec.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There are, of course, none in the province of Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, the situation in Newfoundland is quite distinct. As the hon. member knows, I would imagine, under the terms of confederation there is no differentiation between the various residents of the province of Newfoundland. The Indians and Eskimos are completely integrated into the population.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not want to lead the minister down the garden path. The minister, I think, knows there is no differentiation between the Eskimo and other people of Canada, but only between the Indians and the other people of Canada. The only people who have any special status in any part of Canada are the Indians. It is not because of any special status that anything is being done for the Eskimos, it is because of their remoteness. Most of them, I suppose, before confederation was completed in 1949, lived in the Northwest Territories, not in the provinces. There was no appreciable number of Eskimos in the provinces except in northern Manitoba and Quebec. It may well be that with the entry of Newfoundland into confederation, the majority of the Eskimos, or a considerable proportion of them, are now in the provinces.
I noticed the undertaking the minister gave to my colleague from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador the other day. It does seem to me that there should be equal treatment for the Eskimos in all parts of Canada. It is true that, with respect to the Indians, when confederation was completed in 1949 it was decided not to bring the Indians of Newfoundland under the Indian Act. I think that was a wise decision. Perhaps a mistake was made at that time, which I hope is going to be repaired in time, in that notwithstanding the fact these Indians were not going to come under the Indian Act, they were not, as they should be, treated just as well by the federal government as are other Indians in other parts of Canada. However, I know that is not the minister's responsibility.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to add a few words on this problem, Mr. Chairman. In 1955, I believe, the present minister was a member of the special committee on estimates. It is reported that when we came to the question of education of the Eskimos, Mr. Lesage, the then minister of northern affairs, told the committee he had been in touch with the representatives of both the churches concerned in Canada. Does the minister not feel it would be wise to consult with these authorities before making any plans to educate these Eskimos, and to consult with the Roman Catholic and Anglican churches as Mr. Lesage did in 1955?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am informed that the closest possible consultation continues between the department of northern affairs and the bishops of the respective Anglican and Roman Catholic churches.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There is just one question I should like to ask the minister. Could he say what government was in office in Quebec when these Eskimo schools were established there?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Lesage was minister at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am just trying to discover the date when these schools were opened. It was 1949.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I can answer the question for the minister. If the schools were established in 1949, Mr. Lesage was not a member of the government of Canada. However, Mr. Maurice Duplessis was the premier of Quebec, and that great champion of provincial autonomy permitted the federal government to establish these schools in the province of Quebec. It does seem to me that little bit of history ought to be put on the record.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I know the minister said that the schools in the north are federal schools. He also gave the impression that, in essence, these denominational schools, as he called them I think, in Quebec, were sectarian schools. What I want to know is this. As the educational system develops and as we get into the ambitions of the department as expressed in the annual report to give these Indian children more extensive education at a higher level, for example, as to these technical schools and trade institutes, are they going to continue within the sectarian framework or are they going to be more like, let us say, the schools to which we are accustomed in Manitoba or Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think I should point out that the school situation in the north is rather the result of a historical development. The church missionaries were pioneers in the

north. Both the Roman Catholic church and the Anglican church missionaries were the first to bring education to our northern Canadians. They had established certain priorities in this regard. When the decision was made to provide adequate education for all the young people of Canada's northland, the outstanding contribution of the churches in the north had to be taken into consideration. That is the reason for the denominational criterion with respect to the hiring of teachers.
So far as the vocational schools are concerned, I am happy to inform members that in schools of this type catering to children of the high school level and the teen-age group, we are hoping to move them forward to a completely integrated school. This objective has already been accomplished at Yellowknife. I trust that the hon. member can travel down north on some occasion and I think he will be impressed with the educational program at the Sir John Franklin school at Yellowknife where we have a complete integrated educational program with Indians, Eskimos and white children working side by side as Canadians.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister may remember that one of the recommendations of the parliamentary committee on mines, forests and waters was that arrangements be made to take members of parliament on tours to see these facilities. I am afraid I am not in a position to do this on my own funds. I would have to be, in essence, a freeloader if I were going to do it.
I should like to get back to what the minister has explained and again this is a matter of curiosity. The position in relation to the schools is this. The minister says that we are carrying on historic tradition. However, in essence it is substantiating in religion a status quo. I think he would agree with that statement. I just want to put this question. With regard to education has there been any other denomination or sect interested in proselytizing or doing missionary work in the north? Have they been interested in the present school set-up or have they been critical of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As I indicated just a few minutes ago, the two pioneer churches in the north have been the Anglican church and the Roman Catholic church. No other denomination has expressed any interest in educational programs in the north.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I recognize the hon. member for Scarborough.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have been trying to catch your eye, Mr. Chairman, for quite some time now in order to ask the hon. member for Port
Supply-Northern Affairs Arthur, and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who has been monopolizing the time of the committee here this afternoon, whether they could not pep up their delivery a little bit. I noticed a group of students were falling asleep and the guard was having a difficult time keeping them awake. It was only when the minister started to make his incisive remarks that this tendency was restrained in any way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I will endeavour to oblige the hon. member for York-Scarborough and disturb his own slumbers by reading a little bit of an extract from the May 10, 1960 issue of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald which is rapidly becoming my favourite newspaper. May 10, 1960 was 370 or rather-I am doing my arithmetic the wrong way-360 days ago. Certain events which had not come to an end were then transpiring in the province of Nova Scotia.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It was 370 days ago.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Was I right the first time?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, you were right the first time. Then you made the usual unfortunate mistake of changing it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As a matter of fact, I will leave the arithmetic to the senior member for Halifax or the taller member for Halifax who really does not have much else to keep him occupied since the divorce committee ceased its operations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am keeping you honest; and that is quite a job.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
This item is headed:
"Nowlan Promises Big Power-Net Spending." It is under dateline of Annapolis Royal and it reads as follows:
National Revenue Minister George Nowlan said here Monday night that the federal government planned to spend a large amount this year on the development of power between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
Mr. Nowlan was one-
There is a good deal about where he was speaking and so on. I will spare the minister any embarrassment by failing to identify that. Mr. Nowlan went on to speak about many things that have happened or which he asserted had happened down there and then he went on to say this:
This year, ... it was proposed to spend a large amount on the power pooling project. This would reduce the cost of thermo-power development to less than seven cents per kilowatt.
When we get to the appropriate item

and I am just serving notice on the minister now so that his officials will have a chance to be prepared-I think the committee would be interested in a full report of what has happened in the years since this statement was

Supply-Northern Affairs made and particularly the extent to which the cost of power has been reduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Before this item passes I should like to expand the reply I made to the hon. member for Port Arthur and indicate that the information I gave applied to the Northwest Territories. The Yukon Territory again is another situation. So far as the Indian population is concerned in the Yukon Territory, the hon. member for the Yukon informs me that the Baptist denomination has been very active there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Shall item 279 carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question in order to get an explanation. If I heard him correctly, on two occasions, I think-once since lunch and once before lunch-he indicated that the advertising contracted for by the government and paid for by the government, in respect to that 15 per cent slice off the top to the agency was at no cost to the government. How does he support an argument of that kind, where it is contracted for by the government and paid by the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am informed that this is normal procedure in advertising agencies. Businesses of all kinds and government departments, rather than involve their own personnel in placing these advertisements seek the services of qualified representatives or agencies which have experience in the field. They find that a much more efficient operation can be carried out. The amount of business that is handled by these agencies is in various sums which do not involve any profit so far as the company or the organization or the government placing the advertisement are concerned. They merely indicate that these advertisements are to be placed. The firm or the agency concerned does all the necessary work and the percentage is added to the cost of the medium involved in the advertising. The medium pays a 15 per cent service charge.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am well aware of the mechanics of it but surely the minister is not suggesting that this can be done at no cost to the advertiser. Surely this is a built-in part of the rate which a particular medium might be charging. To suggest that a 15 per cent slice off the top is not paid in the end by the government is, I think, unrealistic.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If the hon. member would consult any reputable advertising agency he would find that this is the practice.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The money comes out of the treasury just the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No. If the government or a company were to place their advertisements directly with the various media it would cost them precisely the same as it would to use the services of an advertising agency.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is a thin argument, when these lush contracts are passed out to the political friends of the minister, to say that it is done at no cost to the federal treasury.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think the only way to put this point across would be to ask the hon. member to approach any advertising agency. I think it would inform him that it is the publicity medium which pays the 15 per cent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am not sure whether the minister qualified one statement which he made-a statement which devastated me- to the effect that only two churches had shown any interest in education in the north, namely the Roman Catholic church and the Anglican church. The Presbyterian church has always prided itself on its interest in education, and to be left in outer darkness is a shattering experience. I wonder if the minister could qualify his statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The Presbyterian church has, of course, been a pioneer in the field of education for many years, even for centuries, but as far as the Northwest Territories are concerned the only two denominations which have been active are the Anglican church and the Roman Catholic church. In the Yukon Territory, going back to the days of the gold rush, I imagine, representatives of the Baptist church have been active among the Indian population. We have two problems in this regard, responsibility for Indian education and responsibility for Eskimo education. I am referring to the Eskimo population. As far as I know there has been no direct participation by the Presbyterian church but I would, of course, agree, that indirectly through various voluntary groups which are now working in northern Canada-the Cana-dian-Eskimo-Indian committee for example which brings together representatives from the women's institutes and various other groups in Canada-there is a genuine interest being shown in all problems with respect to the human resources in our north.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Perhaps I can throw a little light on this question. While what the minister has said is correct, referring to the Northwest Territories as "the north" is using the word "north" in a restricted sense. I was the superintendent general of Indian affairs for three years. I think many people regard northern Ontario and the northern part of the provinces as being the north, as well as the Northwest Territories, and in both those areas the Presbyterian church and the United

Church of Canada have been very active and they have a considerable number of schools there, as well as the Anglican church and the Catholic church.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Last year officials of the department visited the United Kingdom and western Europe in an attempt to assess the tourist potential there in the light of the growing economic strength of those countries. Would the minister now comment on the result of this examination and tell us what is being done to encourage tourist traffic from western Europe?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes. I am glad the hon. member for Nipissing asked this question, because we are pleased with the results of that visit. It was a fact finding trip and I have had reports on the results.
The various Canadian transportation companies have been active in Europe for several years, now-the railways and T.C.A.-and it was found that they are doing an outstanding job in representing Canada. However, strong recommendations were made as a result of the trip that there should be some direct representation of the Canadian government travel bureau in the United Kingdom to serve that market as well as the European market generally.
This whole matter is under very active consideration. We are hoping that at the next tourist convention sponsored by the Canadian government tourist bureau the guest speaker will be one of the leading figures from the tourist industry in the United Kingdom. It is apparent that the best market for increased travel to Canada exists in the United Kingdom, West Germany, the Netherlands, France and Switzerland, to give some specific information which has been brought to my attention as a result of the visit. In all those countries the standard of living has risen remarkably. Foreign exchange restrictions have been lessened or eliminated, and the economies are buoyant. The best possibility for an immediate increase in tourist traffic to Canada is in the United Kingdom. All in all, we can conclude that the tour was successful. The information derived will provide the basis of constructive activity along these lines.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have understood the minister correctly, the government, as a result of this trip or survey last year, has not taken any specific action.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There is nothing before parliament at the present time but we are optimistic that we shall have something to present to the house next year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I should like to associate myself with other hon. members, on behalf
Supply-Northern Affairs of my constituents, and myself, in congratulating the minister upon his appointment to his new office as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. The constituency of Moose Mountain is, of course, in close proximity to that of Brandon-Souris, and this is another reason for wishing the hon. gentleman well in his new post.
Before this item passes I should like to ask the minister a question, and my question is this. Last year I made a discourse in this chamber at some length on the circumstances as far as national parks are concerned. I pointed out that the great central province of Saskatchewan has only one national park whereas some of the neighbouring provinces such as Alberta, and British Columbia have four each. I also pointed out that while the national park of Waskesiu in the northern part of our province is a very fine one it is far distant from the main centres of population. I am wondering whether the department has given any consideration to the expansion of its national park program in the province from which I come.
I should like to direct the minister's attention to another question and it has to do with the possibility of designating Can-nington manor as a historic site. This is a building of an unusual and distinctive type which was put up, I think, in the eighteenth century by English people who established there what might be called a piece of old England. It is equipped with stables, a race track and other adjuncts to elegant English country life; for instance, the sport of hunting was practised around the manor and continued for some time. I thought I should like to bring this matter to the attention of the minister and to ask whether his officials could not consider the possibility of establishing this building as a historic site.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am aware of both the issues referred to by my neighbour across the border in Saskatchewan, and I know of his continuing interest in these matters.
With reference to national parks, I can assure hon. members that the department is always happy to consider suggestions for the expansion of our national parks system. However, one of the basic problems in this regard is that any area to be considered as a national park must be made available by provincial authorities, free of encumbrances. This information is perhaps pertinent to some of the comments made by hon. members from the maritimes. Various suggestions are put forward from time to time regarding areas which might be suitable for national parks, but my department can take no action until the provincial government has first indicated it is willing to turn over the lands for national

Supply-Northern Affairs park purposes. On that basis we are happy to hear representations at any time.
In regard to the Cannington manor, which is a replica of an old English estate in the heart of the prairies going back to the early days of settlement, again this would have to be cleared by the historic sites and monuments board, to determine whether it meets the necessary criteria enabling it to be established as a national historic site. If hon. members can persuade that board in this regard we will be agreeable to taking the necessary steps.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, a few moments ago the minister referred to an overseas delegation in regard to Canada's tourist industry. In this field we have received quite a number of publications originating with this department. I wonder whether the minister could tell me how many of these tourist industry pamphlets are printed in French only, how many in English only, and how many in both French and English?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am informed that up to the present date the activities of the Canadian government travel bureau have been restricted almost to the United States market except for that delegation which was sent to Europe last year. Our operations have been carried out through the offices in New Fork and Chicago. This year, as the hon. member knows, we are going to open a tourist bureau on the west coast of the United States at San Francisco.
Because of this situation, the only demand for tourist publications is received from English speaking areas and pamphlets are designed entirely to serve that market. Of course, when we actively seek to attract European tourists, and if and when we establish a travel bureau in Europe, we will have to consider the problem of cultivating tourists from France and other parts of the continent by the use of multi-language pamphlets and programs.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Does the minister not think that in order to attract Belgians, French, Swiss and perhaps individuals from West Germany, it should be much more effective if our publications were printed in French? I can furnish the minister with a number of bilingual publications, and I suggest our own publications could be printed in both English and French without the loss of any advantage, and without an increase in volume of paper. Perhaps the pamphlets I have would be of assistance to the minister in his consideration regarding the printing of this type of publication in both languages.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I have indicated, when we begin to work directly with


a view to acquiring tourists from Europe we will be faced with the necessity of having bilingual publications, or perhaps trilingual publications. We will be then attempting to cultivate this market in Europe and will have to do so by using the different languages, but up until the present time our operation has been restricted exclusively to the United States market.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Does the minister intend to wait until he has an establishment in Europe before making these publications bilingual? I would suggest there is another consideration involved, and that is, if these publications were printed in French and English the people around the world would realize that Canada is in fact a bilingual country. These people might otherwise think, when they see our publications, that bilingualism in Canada exists only in text books and nowhere else.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this branch operates on a limited budget, and the main interest has been to stimulate the tourist industry in the United States. Many developments are taking place in regard to our tourist promotional program, and I would suggest that as we approach Canada's centennial we will have to considerably broaden the scope of our activity in order to ensure that the true nature of Canada is presented, and our bicultural and bilingual aspects will have to be conveyed to the potential touring public, particularly from Europe. I do not know whether there would be any particular advantage in presenting the bilingual aspect to the United States tourists, but that is something I shall have to consider further.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I would suggest that the advantage involved here would be that of presenting a true picture of Canada to these people from outside, so that they should know there are a number of French speaking Canadians in this country. Regarding the limited budget, to which the minister referred, I should suggest that one of the pamphlets I have in my office contains only one page of pictures and could have been printed in French as well as in English with the addition of one sheet, and the inclusion of French captions under the pictures appearing on that page, with very little cost because of the very small increase in the amount of paper and practically no increase in the amount of ink. This could have been done at no extra cost if someone had only thought about it.
(Translation):

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I would like to put a supplementary question to the minister.
