At the time Mr. Lesage was heading the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, were the Canadian government

travel bureau publications issued in both English and French, even when intended tor the United States? To follow up the question put by the hon. member for Hull, was the literature issued at that time in the United States by the Canadian government travel bureau bilingual or unilingual?
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, these publications have always been printed in one language.
(Translation):

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The question just raised is a purely political one and can hardly improve the situation. I would therefore point out to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) that even if mistakes were made in the past, that is no justification for future governments repeating the same mistakes. On the other hand, if the question raised by the hon. member was merely intended to compare past activities to present activities, he was wrong. We want improvements for the future, even if we have to get them through the present government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not object to what the hon. member for Hull has just said. On the contrary, I favour his suggestion. I feel sure the minister and the officials of his department will consider the question and try to see that Canada be known throughout the world as a bi-ethnic country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Then, how does Mr. Lesage come into the picture?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Lesage has been derelict in his duty.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am prepared to admit that. (Text):

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Order. Shall vote 279 carry?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
281.	Contributions to the provinces, pursuant to agreements entered into with the approval of the governor in council, by Canada with the provinces, of amounts equal to one half of the amounts confirmed by the provinces as having been spent by them for campground and picnic area developments, $1,700,000.
(Translation):

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I understand that item 281 deals with contributions to the provinces on a 50 per cent basis for campground and picnic area developments.
Mr. Chairman, in the last elections, several of our Conservative friends from Quebec denounced all these joint programs as being interference with the autonomy of the provinces. Just recently, the leader of the opposition in Quebec also denounced those
Supply-Northern Affairs programs. So that our Conservative friends from Quebec may clearly indicate whether or not they agree with the policy of the Union Nationale, I see no better way than to call for a vote on the item when the hon. members have completed their remarks. I therefore ask that a vote be taken.
(Text):

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question on this item of $1,700,000. If I understand aright, this has to do with a joint agreement between the dominion government and the provinces. I think the federal government pays one half of the amount of the contribution. Since the inception of this scheme, how much money has been spent by this government and what provinces have entered the joint agreement, including the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this program has been operating since 1958. I believe the hon. member has asked for the total spent since that time. As illustrated in tabular form, up to the end of 1960 the totals were as follows:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What about Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Quebec did not enter the program until the current year. There has been an expenditure on the winter works program of $9,915. There has been no expenditure under the trans-Canada highway program.
Item agreed to: Yeas, 53; nays, nil.
282.	Contributions to the provinces to assist in the development of roads leading to resources in accordance with agreements entered into by Canada and the provinces, $12,000,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like, if I may, to ask the minister whether he would consider a road into Labrador. I have in mind the announcement which he made in the house on Wednesday, part of which said in effect that where there are two companies operating in the northland the federal government would build a road to that area and pay 100 per cent of the cost. I should like to call his attention to the fact that in Carol lake and lake Wabush, which is one area in Labrador, there are two big mining developments. I would be very happy indeed if the minister would tell us that he is going to build a road from, say, the north shore

Supply-Northern Affairs of the St. Lawrence into that area, or from Goose Bay into that area, which would make me happier still.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the roads to resources program applies, of course, only to the provinces. The announcement I made the other day concerned our access road program in the territories where the federal government has exclusive responsibility. Under the roads to resources program we accept recommendations from the provincial governments and these recommendations are processed for the necessary criteria pertaining to roads to resources. We are happy to entertain any recommendation by the provincial governments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the end of the discussion of this item I should like you to call the yeas and nays because this important item relates to a large amount of money, namely $12 million.
I should like to know first from the minister how much money has been spent by the government under this kind of subvention to the provinces? I should like to have a breakdown of the amount by provinces up to the present time.
The minister knows that since the inception of this agreement the province of Quebec has always refused to enter into an agreement with the federal government because the premier of the province held that it was an encroachment on provincial autonomy. I know that all the Conservative members from Quebec and even the Conservative ministers from that province campaigned in the provincial elections on behalf of Maurice Duples-sis who always objected to these agreements. I should like to know how they could tell the people of Quebec that this was an encroachment on the autonomy of that province and then come into this house and say they were in favour of this encroachment on the autonomy of the province of Quebec. If they do not want this item to pass because it is an encroachment on the autonomy of Quebec, I wonder why they would vote for it? If they do not approve of the previous governments of the province of Quebec they should say so.
Every time we come to items of this kind we never hear from these Conservative members from the province of Quebec. They are very brave when they are talking to a Conservative meeting in the province of Quebec. I even heard the hon. member for Chapleau say over the radio that under this administration millions of dollars had been given through him for the development of access roads. Nevertheless, when a meeting is held by Mr. Talbot of the Union Nationale the hon. member is beside Mr. Talbot and denouncing agreements of this kind. I should like to know whether their stand is "Yes" here and "No"
in Quebec or vice versa. On what side of the fence do they stand? At the end of the discussion of this item I should like the yeas and nays to be called. I would ask the minister to give us the amounts of money by provinces spent under this program.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words because the hon. member for St. Denis mentioned the fact that in a radio broadcast recently I said that large amounts of money had been spent and most of it, I am glad to say, in the north in the riding of Chapleau on the roads to resources program which is under discussion now. He implied that members of the Conservative party campaigned for the provincial party in the last election. I wish to say that we are discussing federal matters here. As far as I am concerned, I have said that these amounts are being spent and there is no question in my mind that they will help in the development of the north country. I do not think we should mix provincial matters with federal matters and I will be glad to vote in favour of this item.
(Translation):

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, with reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Martel), I must say that the province of Quebec must necessarily be included in this discussion, since the expenditures involved in this item could not be made unless the province of Quebec agrees to share half the cost. A matter of principle is involved. Therefore, if you say that this constitutes an infringement upon autonomy and if, at your meetings in the province of Quebec, you denounce this item, I wonder why you vote in favour of it in this house. Either you change your mind, or-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We are not here to discuss provincial politics.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is not one law for one's friends and another for one's foes.
I am unable to understand, Mr. Chairman, how these people can boast to their constituents that they are the protectors of autonomy.
(Text):

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Order. If the hon. member for Chapleau had presented his case in the form of a point of order I would be inclined to agree that the debate on this item has strayed from the point which is the subject of inquiry from the minister and I would have to ask the hon. member for St. Denis to restrict his references to another arena which has no jurisdiction as far as this expenditure is concerned.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I have the breakdown I requested?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes. Would the hon. member be satisfied with round figures?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
These figures are up until the end of 1960: British Columbia, $2,200,000; Alberta, $2,300,000; Saskatchewan, $2,600,000; Manitoba, $1,700,000; Ontario, $1,300,000; Quebec, nil; New Brunswick, $1,200,000; Nova Scotia, almost $3 million; Prince Edward Island, $1,700,000, and Newfoundland almost $516,000.
(Translation):

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I find that the Quebec Tories cost the province a lot of money.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That might be a lesson for Mr. Lesage, who was against those subsidies but finally accepted them.
(Text):

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
May I say we were never opposed to these agreements. Premier Lesage hoped for the disappearance of these joint agreements little by little but would not refuse our share while they existed.
(Translation):
We shall accept all that the federal government gives the provinces. We shall have our share in the amounts of money distributed throughout the country. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) has paid his taxes; well he is entitled to his share of the amounts being spent under this item. Surely, he did not fail to notice the millions that were spent to the benefit of other provinces while the province of Quebec lagged behind during the time when the Union Nationale ruled the destinies of the province.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Your attitude shows you to favour centralization of power.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Just vote against this item if it is contrary to your principles.
(Text):

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Could the minister give the committee a list of the projects approved under this program in the current year for the province of New Brunswick?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It is quite a long list, and I am happy to give it to the hon. member. The roads are as follows: the Juniper-Napadogan road, the Plaster Rock-Renous road, the Doaktown-Chipman road, the Blue River road, the Maces Bay road, the Saint John-Mispec road, the north central New Brunswick resources roads, the Boiestown or Doaktown to Plaster Rock road, the Kingston peninsula loop, the Bayfield-Mates Corner road, the Grand Lake road, the Salmon river bridge, the cape Bald loop, the Shediac bay loop, the Buctouche bay loop, the Richibucto loop
Supply[DOT]-Northern Affairs and the St. Croix river road. These are the projects that have been approved.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Has the minister received a request covering a road to Miscou island, including a bridge linking Shippigan island and Miscou, and what action has been taken on this project?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I understand there have been requests for two additional road projects including the one mentioned by the hon. member, the other being a mining development road into the Heath Steel Company development. These two are under consideration at the moment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Could I ask the minister whether he was right in giving the figure for Nova Scotia which seemed almost astronomical compared with the other provinces? I think all the other provinces were under $2 million and Nova Scotia was over $3 million. I just wondered whether the figure he gave was correct and, if so, where these roads are.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I now have a more up-to-date report. The first report was to the end of December, 1960, and the one I have in my hands now is to the end of January, 1961. The figure given for Nova Scotia is $3,032,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is higher than any other province.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, Alberta is higher with $3,200,000. Those are the two highest provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: But it is higher than Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario or British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder whether the minister can tell me about a road in which I am particularly interested, that from Gypsum-ville to Grand Rapids? Has that road been finished and is it intended to continue it farther north to Thompson?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I believe the hon. member is referring to Manitoba again and discussing the Manitoba roads to resources program.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is the item under discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The road from Gypsumville, I understand, was officially opened at Christmas. I understand that it represents the longest piece of road developed in the shortest space of time in Canadian history. It is now

Supply-Northern Affairs proceeding to Thompson and when it gets to Thompson we will be only 200 miles from the port of Churchill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I believe in the original agreement with the province of Ontario in connection with the roads to resources program there were eight projects listed at a total cost of $8,360,000. Would the minister tell us how many of those roads have been completed under this program and the cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, I have that information. The Savant lake south road: there has been no activity on this road to date. The Foyelet to Chapleau road: 23 miles have been cleared. The Minaki south road: 15 miles have been cleared out of a total of 15 miles. The Nakina northerly road, a total distance of 50 miles: I have not got the report of the work completed, but there has been a total of $429,268 paid out on that project. Goldpines to Uchi lake; there has been no activity on that project. Port Arthur north, a total distance of 70 miles: 28 miles have been cleared.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What has happened in connection with the Campbell mine to Red lake road and No. 8 northern service? This was a very short road of about two miles.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: According to my records here, Mr. Chairman, the Campbell to Red lake road is not part of the roads to resources agreement. I believe the hon. member is referring to the road that was discussed by the hon. member for Port Arthur last night. This road is described in the agreement between the federal government and the government of Ontario, the form of road to be agreed upon after completion of photographic and magnetometer surveys. In addition, some geological reconnaissance will be carried out. I am happy to inform the hon. member that the major portion of the preliminary work has been completed. All the aeromagnetic work is completed and maps have been published. About 60 per cent of the ground geological work has been completed, and the balance will be done this year. It is expected that a detailed road location can commence later during the current year, and it is hoped the actual construction will commence in 1962.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Can the minister tell us if there are any negotiations currently under way to extend other roads in other areas not included in the roads to resources program? In other words, are there negotiations taking place between the provincial and federal governments to extend these roads into other areas beyond those initially projected in the province of Ontario? I am thinking, for instance, of a road from Gowganda to either the Chapleau

or Sudbury area. Another road that has been mentioned on a number of occasions is a road north from Cochrane to Moosonee and also one north from Kapuskasing to serve the area north of Kapuskasing.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the roads I have outlined are the complete projects under the present agreement. There are no further negotiations taking place at the present time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I wish to follow the hon. member for Timiskaming because he referred to certain roads in my riding. I do not believe the population of Cochrane are so anxious to know about new roads from Timmins to Kapuskasing or Kapuskasing to Moosonee. They are anxious to learn about a road that would connect the northwestern part of Quebec with the northeastern part of Ontario. I wonder if the minister could tell me if there are any suggestions from the provincial governments concerning the possibility of opening up that area, 52 miles in length, between northwestern Quebec and La Reine and Cochrane. This would be the road in which the population of that district would be interested. They want this road as a tourist road, as a road to resources and also as a necessary road in case of attack on this country.
After all, the northern part of the province is quite a distance from Toronto and some 300 miles north of North Bay. The only real outlet we would have in case of attack would be to the west to Port Arthur and Fort William or east into Quebec province. This road would be a most important one to the population of my riding, and the one in which they would be most interested.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I can inform the hon. member that we have received no representations concerning this road.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am very interested in this item because I am interested in these roads to resources. I might say that I have been interested in some hot springs for 50 years, the Nakusp hot springs which are nine miles northeast of Nakusp. I have been a commissioner of the park committee that has been formed since 1925, but we have no road to these hot springs. They are equal to radium springs. About 70,000 gallons of water come out of the ground every 24 hours at a temperature of about 134. We have two others very similar within a distance of 40 miles. There are magnificent opportunities for bathing and the establishment of a resort. Over 35 miles of the finest brook trout fishing in Canada, as well as magnificent scenery, can be found there.

For years, the people have either walked or rode a horse over the nine mile trail to these springs. Prior to the second world war there would be anywhere from 600 to 800 people visiting these springs annually, enjoying the baths, the fishing and the scenery. People seem to have gotten out of the habit of riding and walking since the second world war, so the numbers that come now are very reduced. We have been very interested in getting a road built over the nine miles required to service these magnificent hot springs.
I want to ask the minister three questions. I have tried to explain briefly the type of natural resource this is. Does the government contribute to the construction of roads to this type of natural resource if a province makes application? Has the government of British Columbia made application for assistance in building a road to these hot springs? Can the minister go through the list of projects that have been undertaken in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In response to the first question may I say this. The federal government accepts recommendations from the provincial government for resource roads. The answer to the second question is this. The provincial government made no representations concerning the road referred to. As a matter of fact, I think the only road project in the province of British Columbia in the roads to resources program is the Stewart-Cassiar road. They have put the whole amount of money available into one project.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I want to thank the minister for that information. It will brew a good storm in the Kootenays.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I wish to add a few words to those of the hon. member for Cochrane with regard to the road suggested for northern Ontario to connect northeastern Ontario with northwestern Quebec. Some work has been done in that respect by-and the hon. member may correct me if I am wrong-the northern Ontario development association. There have been meetings with the Abitibi chamber of commerce and also the chamber of commerce of La Sarre. Our people in Quebec are also greatly interested in that road. I believe as well that some work has been done for that purpose, namely to build that road. Of course the suggestion will have to come from the Ontario government because on the Quebec side the road goes to the border. It all depends on what road will be chosen. However, it will be only a matter of few miles, possibly five miles at the most, depending on where this road will go.
I think it would be well for the minister if he would inquire whether his department

maintopic: CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF AGE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-25, to amend the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act (age discrimination).

He said: My remarks in connection with this particular bill will be brief. The Fair Employment Practices Act has been on the statute books for some years. It prohibits discrimination with regard to the employment of employees, among other things in so far as membership in trade unions is concerned. The act provides that discrimination shall not be practised on the basis of race, national origin, colour or religion.
What this bill seems to do is to add the further provision that discrimination shall not be practised because of the age of the prospective employee or of the employee unless age is considered to be a bona fide occupational factor. The bill seeks to deal at the present time with the question of membership in unions and the proposed amendment would merely add another provision in respect to age unless, as I say, that is a bona fide occupational factor. There are, in addition, those other matters such as race, national origin, colour and religion with which the act is already concerned.
I think we are all aware that discrimination has existed and exists right now among employers with regard to the age of individuals employed. We have all heard cases where a person of 40 years of age, or 45 or 50-the age varies with the industry and the circumstances-has been unable to gain employment because he is considered to be too old. In some instances the reason is given that an older person becomes less efficient and tends to slow down on the job. Another reason given, and I think it is the most prevalent, arises from the growth of pension plans in industry. A number of industries find that it is difficult to fit an older worker into a pension plan because by the time he reaches the normal retirement age in that industry he will not have put in enough service to qualify for a pension, or, in other words, the contributions to the pension fund made by himself, or on his behalf by the employer, or jointly, would not be sufficient to qualify him for a pension, or at any rate for an adequate pension.
We have advocated, of course, on other occasions and in other circumstances that a portable pension system should be instituted so as to allow a worker to take his pension plan with him when he moves from one job to another, thus enabling him to work in a number of different industries over a period of years. But that is another subject and I think it would not be proper except in a general way to debate that during the discussion of this particular bill.
Unfortunately these pension barriers, along with other factors, deprive people of the right to gainful employment, for no real valid, sensible or sound reason. This bill 90205-6-280
Fair Employment Practices Act seeks to overcome that particular situation. There are a number of other places in the world where such anti-discrimination laws exist but I do not think it is necessary for me to list the states which have this legislation on their statute books or to recount the experiences they have had in those places. Nevertheless, the material is on the files and the experience of anti-discrimination legislation may be consulted.
In support of my statement that discrimination does exist and of my contention that changes should be made I should like to qoute from the remarks of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr 1 as contained in a booklet published in 1960 by the Queen's printer entitled "Speaking Out about the Older Worker Problem". This is a publication containing some 26 pages. It deals extensively with the problem of the older workers from a variety of viewpoints. Within its pages, as I said, is a statement by the Minister of Labour, who has this to say as reported on pages 7 and 8 of the booklet:
Justice, and freedom of opportunity to every individual, as spelled out by the United Nations, was adopted by 58 countries, including Canada, in the universal declaration of human rights, in December 1948. Is it justice and freedom of opportunity to raise obstacles to employment against any segment of society, for any reason, including age? Should not all individuals have an equal right to jobs which they are capable of doing whether they are 20 or 70 years of age?
The second paragraph I wish to read from page 8 is as follows:
In the Department of Labour and the national employment service we contend that applicants for jobs should be hired on the basis of character, ability and qualifications needed for the particular job, and that age should not be a factor. It is because many persons in their forties or fifties are turned down for jobs simply because of age- even though fully qualified-that we have the social and economic problem of the older worker.
Mr. Speaker, these words of the Minister of Labour add weight, if that is necessary, to the reasons why this particular bill should be endorsed by all hon. members and placed on the statute books of our country.

maintopic: CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not have any association in mind. These words were taken from the phraseology used in similar legislation in other jurisdictions. Apparently individuals had been faced with this peculiar situation and adopted this method of solving the problem, so as to prevent any implication of a restriction as to age. Perhaps as an illustration I could suggest that, if a group of employees working in a home for the aged called themselves the national union of employees for the home for the aged, there would be no possibility of discrimination because of the name itself under legislation based on this bill.

maintopic: CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF AGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so far as this bill serves to draw attention to the plight of the older workers it has a useful purpose. However, as in many circumstances where we are dealing with prejudice, it is very difficult to draft legislation to prevent it. I suggest that we must educate the general public as to the usefulness of older workers.
As has been mentioned on numerous occasions, there are many prejudices in Canada and elsewhere throughout the world relating to the usefulness of persons who have reached a certain age. I hope this discussion today will put forward a case for the older worker. The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) on several occasions has presented this case for the older worker. He did so last year during a very forthright discussion regarding the whole problem.
There are two main problems facing the older worker. The first is an economic problem, and the second can be classed as a prejudicial problem. In many institutions employers hesitate to hire individuals who will shortly be entitled to retirement and drawing pensions, or other retirement allowances, for the obvious economic reasons. Second, even though an individual may offer to work without the benefit of a retirement plan, he would be in a very difficult position. Many older people on occasion will volunteer, because they realize that they will not be working for a very long period of time, to waive their pension rights. This proposal has never been acceptable because it would result in different treatment from different employers. This type of offer made by older workers, to get around the difficulty, has met with little success.


Regarding the problem of prejudice facing older people, I would suggest there is a feeling among employers, in regard to giving jobs to older people, that they are not as efficient as* younger people. I would suggest this is not always true. We should first consider what the prejudices are that an older worker must face. I shall attempt to list several of them which I feel are among the foremost. The first, is that when workers grow older their ability to learn decreases and therefore it is more difficult to train them in newer industrial and technological techniques. Second, a man over 40 is presumed not to be as productive as he was at 20. Third, the frequency of illness increases with age and there is more absenteeism among older workers than among younger workers. Fourth, physical deterioration is synonomous with age and therefore older people are accident prone. Finally, age has a direct bearing on insurance rates, and the cost of pension plans increases with each new participant over 40 years of age.
Those prejudices I have outlined represent the beliefs of a considerable number of employers, although it is generally accepted that these are not true statements of the facts. These beliefs are not necessarily accurate in respect of individuals 40 years and older, but are myths regarding older workers.
Mr. Speaker, I received a mimeographed letter last year, as I imagine all hon. members did, from a Mr. George D. Glassford of 132 Central Park boulevard north, Oshawa, Ontario, dated March 7, 1960. This gentleman set forth his particular problem in this letter, and I should like to read two paragraphs. They are as follows:
Business, big and small, American or Canadian controlled; governments, federal, provincial and municipal, are all tarred with the same brush.
They'll deny it emphatically-show examples where the statement is wrong-but the pitifully few examples they can show have resulted from pressure-executive, customer, or political-in each individual case. Rarely is one ever turned down because of age, as such. That would never do. The reasons are many and varied and often far fetched. I should know. I've been getting them for 15 months.
This letter was written by a man who states that he is almost 60 and was born in Canada. He had service in the first war. He goes through a long list of jobs that he has held but he says his difficulty now is his age. His letter points up the problem but I do not think it points up the answer and I do not think it necessarily points to the bill that we are discussing.
This writer says that age is never given to him as the real reason for not employing him. He says he receives these other reasons which are varied, but employers never come up with the statement that it is really his age which

is causing the difficulty. In such a situation the provisions of Bill No. C-25 would not help very much, because it would still remain possible for an employer to use the same reasons that he is using now and never mention age. To this extent I am not sure that the bill would actually accomplish the purpose the hon. member has in mind.
When I was looking up my notes on this bill in anticipation of speaking I went through a file I have of people who write to me looking for employment. I am not going to quote those letters directly but I have extracted statements from them over a period of the last two years which illustrate this particular problem. One letter says, "Everywhere I go I am told I am too old". Then, in brackets he says, " I am 56 years old". Another letter says, "At my age, 52, positions are hard to obtain". Another letter contains this sentence, "I am 57 years old and have still got six children to support, some of which are still going to school. Now, at 57 years old, I find it very hard to get work". In another letter dated July of last year I find this sentence, "Now, what am I to do at 54 years old to find a job?" These are four extracts that I took from those letters. I do not receive a great many letters asking for employment, but from that number I managed to select four letters, the writers of which definitely stated their real problem was age and nothing else.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on this bill I find myself in substantial agreement with what has just been said by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. I was rather surprised at the introductory remarks of the mover of the bill, the hon. member for Skeena, but he did not deal with one of the aspects raised by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, namely we all recognize that the subject matter of the bill presents a problem. The hon. member for Skeena did not deal at any length with how he felt this particular bill would overcome the problem.

maintopic: CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF AGE
speechtext: I will do that when I close the debate.

maintopic: CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF AGE
speechtext:
I
should think that would be the first consideration we should want to have before us. Before we undertook to enact any such measure we should want to be sure that it was going to have the desired effect. It seems a rather odd time to do it at the end of the debate when hon. members would not have the benefit of the views of the hon. member for Skeena on the subject.
It does seem to me that this bill not only would not overcome the problem with which we have to deal but in fact it perhaps might raise a lot of other problems. For instance, many firms have a pension plan which, as has been pointed out, is designed to provide a man with a retirement income on which he may retire at age 65. As I see it, under the terms of this bill, if a company had a pension plan of that nature and expected its employees to retire at age 65, then that would be discriminatory if the employee declined to resign at 65. He would perhaps feel within his rights to stay there until he was 85 or so long as he was able to work. That aspect of the matter would certainly have to be taken into consideration.
Then again, I think a firm would have many legitimate reasons for wanting a person of a certain age for a particular job. In the explanatory note of this bill I see that the mover has said:
The chief purpose of this bill is to add age discrimination to the list of prohibited employment practices unless age is a bona fide occupational qualification.
I do not know exactly what the definition of a bona fide occupational qualification would be.
Then, the hon. member goes on to say:
A secondary purpose is to prohibit the employer from including in an employment application form, advertisement or written or oral inquiry, a question or request for particulars as to the applicant's -race, national origin, colour, religion or age unless by reason of a bona fide occupational qualification.

Fair Employment Practices Act
It seems to me that a firm would have to take into consideration the average age of its staff. For instance, in the case of a small firm, it might have a small office staff of half a dozen employees, three or four of whom may be getting on toward retirement age. Of course, if that firm was looking to the future it certainly would not want to hire another person who was getting on toward retirement age; it would be looking for someone who would be with the firm for a number of years and would then have the training to carry on. It seems to me that in a case of that kind a firm would have a legitimate reason. Whether it would come within the terms of a bona fide occupational qualification, I do not know. It certainly would not be a good idea if that could be said to be a bona fide occupational qualification. An older person could very well do the job and therefore it could hardly be said to be a bona fide occupational qualification.
For that reason I believe that this particular amendment to prevent discrimination against older workers, with the principle of which I agree, would not in fact overcome the problem. I believe that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has already taken some very constructive action with regard to the matter. I know that about two years ago I received at my office in my firm in Vancouver a letter sent out by the Minister of Labour in which he drew the attention of many thousands of employers across the country to the problem. I have a copy here and I believe it had a very good effect on firms. As a result of this letter and other actions he has taken, such as setting up a small group under the civilian rehabilitation branch of the Department of Labour to deal with this specific subject, in my opinion he has done a great deal to help to alleviate the situation.
There have been reports that employers have paid attention to the requests of the Department of Labour to try to take some measures to overcome the problem. I notice it is reported that several employers have initiated special savings plans by payroll deduction for new employees who may be too old to enter a pension plan. That was one of the difficulties, and if that scheme could be expanded it would, of course, do a great deal to overcome the problem.
A number of publications have been issued by the Department of Labour and other branches of the government, and I think it might be a good idea to put some of them on the record so that people who are interested in the subject will be able to look at some of the information that has been collected. The following publications have been made available from 1957 to the present time: Pension Plans and the Employment of Older

Workers, 1957, sponsored by the interdepartmental committee on older workers and published by the Department of Labour; Research on the Problem of the Employment of the Older Worker, 1958, by Professor S. D. Clark, University of Toronto, sponsored and published by the economics and research branch, Department of Labour; The Aging Worker in the Canadian Economy, 1959, published by the economics and research branch, Department of Labour; Age and Performance in Retail Trade, 1959, published by the economics and research branch, Department of Labour; The Employability of the Older Worker, 1959, by Professor S. D. Clark, University of Toronto, sponsored and published by the economics and research branch, Department of Labour.
There are others here but I think that is a pretty good list for anyone who is interested in the subject. As I said at the commencement of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, while I am certainly not unsympathetic to the stated purpose of the bill which is to prevent discrimination against older workers, I am in no way convinced that the bill will do anything in that regard at all. In fact, I feel very strongly that not only will it not end any problems but it will raise many new ones.
As was so very well pointed out by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken), there are very few instances where a man is told that he is being rejected on account of his age, and it would be most difficult to prove discrimination in that regard. Therefore I think the approach that the Minister of Labour has taken and the very active educational campaign he has carried on are a much more satisfactory solution, and I believe that if all members get behind the minister's program and support him in his efforts to try to encourage employers throughout the country to employ older workers we will be doing a more constructive job than we would by passing this bill.

maintopic: CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF AGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to say a few words with respect to this private member's bill and in commencing my remarks I want to say that, like most hon. members, I am in agreement with the principle of the bill. However, I have reservations as to whether or not Bill No. C-25 would be effective in practice.
Hon. members well realize that in 1953 parliament passed the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. Section 4 of that act sets out certain employment practices that are prohibited including discrimination on the ground of race, national origin, colour or religion. This bill attempts to add the word "age" to the prohibitions. I am wondering what would be the effect of adding "age"

to this section. Would it mean that certain employers, as stated by a previous speaker, would be obligated to continue employees in employment regardless of whether they had reached age 65 or the pensionable age? I suggest in any case that the bill before us would certainly need further amendment to remove that factor.
Another thing that concerns me is whether or not the words "occupational qualification" should be defined in the bill. Everyone has a general idea of the meaning but as the main act covers such a variety of occupations including working on railways, canals, aerodromes, air transportation, banking, broadcasting and practically every type of national employment it would require a huge list of regulations to set out the various occupational qualifications for each particular type of employment which would be affected by the main act. Consequently it would be most difficult, if not impossible, for the director to formulate regulations.
I think the only way to overcome the problem that Canada faces with reference to the plight of people in middle age who become unemployed is for the government and industry to conduct an educational program in a more strenuous manner. The last speaker mentioned certain publications issued by the Department of Labour. I hope the department will continue the distribution of this literature and will accelerate its efforts in that regard. I understand that the radio labour program, "Canada at Work", has mentioned this subject on many broadcasts and I commend the program for doing so. However, education of the people is not going to solve the problem. I suggest that more action on the part of the federal government might be welcomed at this time.
I might mention, for example, the Department of National Defence. All of us have constituents and friends in the permanent forces. Too many of them are compelled to retire on pension at ages when they are still capable of performing adequate service to the crown. I do not suggest that a man in the infantry who is on active training in peacetime can continue to give good service as an officer, non-commissioned officer or other rank beyond the age of 50 but surely it should be possible for the defence department to absorb some of these people in work where less strenuous exercise is involved and to keep them so employed.
At the present time large numbers of military people are retired daily, and a great many of them are entitled to veterans' preference because they stayed in the forces after the end of hostilities. Although national defence no longer employs them, under the
Fair Employment Practices Act Civil Service Act they are entitled to preference if they served overseas and the civil service commission has no choice but to offer them further employment in the government service. In many instances, civil servant applicants who are well qualified are displaced. I make this suggestion to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) because I think it is very closely related to the problem of the older worker today.
Another step which perhaps might correct the situation better than this bill would be the introduction by industry, with government assistance and co-operation, of what are known as portable pensions. I am quite certain, Mr. Speaker, that portable pensions would play a part in solving the occupational problems of people who are unemployed at age 45 and over.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I am in agreement with the principle of this bill. However, I do not see how it would be possible to properly police the measure, and if laws cannot be enforced they should not be put on the statute books. To reiterate what I have just said, I feel that the government should take a close and serious look at the problems created by early retirement from the Department of National Defence. If necessary, perhaps the government should also give serious consideration to the plight of people over 40 who are unemployed because of the fact their jobs have disappeared as a result of automation. It might be possible to give some sort of statutory preference to these citizens who could be trained under the vocational training scheme to take up occupations which would lead to employment with the government.
I want to commend the hon. member for introducing this bill because it gives parliament an opportunity to discuss this serious problem, a problem for which every elected representative in all levels of government has a responsibility in order that this social injustice will be eliminated once and for all in Canada.

maintopic: CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF AGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, like the previous speakers, am in favour of the principle of the bill. I will try to point out what I feel to be the intent of the sponsor of this bill, and the fact that I believe he would have been better advised to introduce a separate bill instead of amending the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. I am in agreement with the thoughts which have been expressed that the government might do more with regard to their own advertising for recruits for the civil service. If they were to put in big letters the information that no age qualifications are necessary for the job, that might help. If

Fair Employment Practices Act ages are ever requested, candidates should only be asked whether they are over 18 and under 65.
I believe other speakers have pointed out that the Department of Labour and the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) have conducted intensive campaigns to educate industry to the advantages of employing older workers. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) mentioned certain of the objections to employing older workers. It has been shown that these are really prejudices which have no foundation in fact. The older worker can be quite as productive as the younger worker because in our industry today we are machine operators rather than pick and shovel operators. There would be less rather than more absenteeism because the older workers are more dependable. In many cases, the older worker is the best bet for the employer.
In considering this proposal to amend the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, our attention should be directed to the nature and purposes of the existing legislation which forbids refusal of employment to a person because of his race, national origin, colour or religion. In endorsing the democratic principle of equality of opportunity in employment, the law prevents denial of the essential oneness of the human family in respect of the right of the individual to seek and find work. The question arising from the proposed amendment is whether or not it should be added as an additional factor to these factors which, by law, are eliminated as obstacles to employment. This proposal is, therefore, timely because it reminds us that there is discrimination in regard to age. I feel, however, that an amendment to the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act does not accomplish our purpose of eliminating this particular discrimination.
It is relatively easy to determine whether there is discrimination with regard to race, national origin, colour or religion. It is not so easy, in fact it would be almost impossible under certain circumstances, to determine whether there is discrimination because of age. For example, if a man of 45 is hired, is another applicant of 46 being discriminated against? Age is a common factor; it is common to everyone. As this act now stands on the statute books, it prevents discrimination because of factors which can be readily determined. In the present act the basis of the legislative provisions relates to race, national origin, colour and religion. Equal employment opportunities for the members of minority racial or religious groups is quite a different consideration from safeguarding the employment opportunities of age groups.


If it is the intention of this amendment to protect the older worker, it fails in its purpose because there is nothing in it which restricts the protection to the older worker. As the proposal now stands, a young person could complain and dislodge an older person from employment, regardless of other practical or economic considerations. There is only one clause in this bill, and if this amendment were to carry it would add age to the other grounds upon which discrimination should not be practised. The clause, in part, would say that there shall be no discrimination because of race, national origin, colour, religion or age unless age is a bona fide occupational qualification. In my opinion, this weakens the principle of the bill as it now exists. Therefore I say that it would be much better if the hon. member for Skeena would not try to accomplish his purpose by amending this present statute and that he should rather bring in a bill which would cover discrimination with regard to age and which might bring in other points such as the portability of pensions or other factors which discriminate against the employment of older people. There is already in Canada and in many other countries of the world legislation which permits distinctions in work in relation to age particularly in connection with night work and underground work which is prohibited for minors. It would appear that there is discrimination on the basis of age, and age being the general and universal factor it is, one must secure a method other than that which is proposed in order to eliminate this discrimination.
There is in Canada, as well as in some other countries, an active program through such agencies as the national employment service encouraging employers to employ the older worker. Education and encouragement would appear to be by far the better way of dealing with the problem rather than through legislation unless that legislation can be so worded as to make it clear cut and not subject to wrong interpretation.
It might be interesting, Mr. Speaker, to look at the experience of other countries and even other provinces of Canada with regard to legislation dealing with discrimination. The
I.L.O. committee on discrimination in the field of employment and occupation in 1957 considered this question of discrimination because of age. A vote on the inclusion of age as a basis was rejected by a vote of 109 to 206 with 67 abstentions. In Canada, none of those provinces with fair employment practices legislation includes age as a basis for discrimination. To the knowledge of the Department of Labour, no country in the world has

positive legislation at the national level which makes age a basis for discrimination in fair employment practices legislation.
I understand that in the United States there are some 10 states which have on their statute books legislation relating to the employment of older workers. In six of these states such a provision is included in the state's fair employment practices act. Here is an interesting point. How do these states define age? Massachusetts defines age as from 45 to 65; Pennsylvania defines age as between 40 and 62; the Connecticut and Wisconsin acts refer to persons 40 and 65 and the Oregon act to those between 25 and 65. Rhode Island's prohibition is in a separate act which defines age to mean between 45 and 65.
From the references I have given I think it will be clear to all hon. members and, I hope, to the sponsor of the bill, that discrimination with regard to age is something that is almost impossible to define by statute. It is like trying to bring in legislation to outlaw evil. That is not to say that we should not try to do something about this matter. However, I believe the methods now being used- I refer to the method of education; the method of persuasion now being used by the Department of Labour; the letters from the minister mentioned by the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway-will have gradually better and more beneficial results.
I think it is rather difficult for members of parliament, so many of whom are professional people whose highest earnings may start at age 60, to understand the plight of the worker who, through the closure of a plant or through technological changes, is thrown out of a job after the age of 45. These men in many cases are not even given the benefit of an interview. They are rejected on the basis of age. This is not right. It is not even good management on the part of the managers of industrial enterprises to take this stand. Therefore, as I say, the idea of this bill is good, but it should be in the form of a separate bill. Therefore, although I am not talking out this bill, I now move the adjournment of this debate.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in our opinion he has neither leave to revert to motions nor leave to make the motion which he is now making and, if I am allowed to do so, I will give the reasons why.
